Sports.title: FA chiefs should be embarrassed by their prior support of disgraced Gianni Infantino
Sports.content:
The Football Association will write a letter revoking its endorsement of Gianni Infantino’s re-election. To which there is one obvious reaction. Why on earth did they ever endorse him?

There will be - there should be - some shamed faces in the FA’s executive ranks right now. The photograph of the FA chair presenting Infantino with a personalised England shirt during the World Cup is not one Debbie Hewitt will want to see again.

But there has been a long line of FA chairs and chief executives who have been happy to go along with Infantino’s regime. In theory, the FA should have one of the most powerful voices in world football but, effectively, it has been silent during a decade in which his tenure has become increasingly embarrassing.

Gianni Infantino and Donald Trump meeting not happening as third nation calls out FIFA boss READ MORE :

The FA’s endorsement of Infantino came after he had turned World Cup football into a game of four quarters. It came after he had given Donald Trump a ‘peace prize’ on behalf of FIFA.

‌



It came after he had somehow managed to allow Saudi Arabia to be unopposed as hosts of the 2034 World Cup. It came after he had sanctioned the outrageous prices most had to pay for World Cup tickets. It came after THAT half-time show.

The FA should never have endorsed his re-election in the first place. They were not alone, of course.

In fact, it appeared there was only going to be the possibility of one or two dissenters when it came to the formality of re-electing Infantino. Now, of course, any possibility of Infantino being re-elected has been blown out of the water.

View 3 Images Gianni Infantino gave Donald Trump the FIFA Peace Prize in December (Image: PA)

‌



In terms of revoking endorsement, the Welsh set the ball rolling when it released a statement on Monday morning. It read: “The Football Association of Wales hereby confirms its withdrawal of support for the candidature of Mr Gianni Infantino for re-election as FIFA president for the 2027-31 term.

“The recent failures in good governance, processes, leadership, values, stakeholder management, communications and sound judgement have led us to a position where Mr Infantino has lost the confidence of the FAW to remain at the helm of world football. Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept.”

Again, the obvious response is to wonder how he had their confidence in the first place. Nevertheless, the withdrawal of endorsements - while largely symbolic - should confirm this is the end for Infantino’s reign.

View 3 Images Gianni Infantino has no way back at FIFA (Image: Getty Images)

‌



UEFA have even written to him, demanding no paperwork relating to the scheme - which would have seen FIFA sell rights to the World Cup to private investors - is destroyed and reserving the right to take legal action. The Prime Minister, Andy Burnham, has called on his to step down.

As it still stands, Infantino plans to stand for re-election at a congress in Morocco in March and would need 106 votes from the 211 member nations to stay in his job.

But with UEFA and CONCACAF already releasing strong statements criticising his leadership, the chances of Infantino’s time in charge of FIFA being extended are extremely slim. In fact, they are surely non-existent.

Sports.title: Southampton boss Tonda Eckert says he received death threats after Spygate scandal
Sports.content:
Southampton boss Tonda Eckert says he received death threats after Spygate scandal

Tonda Eckert became public enemy number one after authorising a junior Southampton staff member to spy on opponents' training sessions last season

View 2 Images Tonda Eckert remains in charge of Southampton (Image: Matt Watson/Southampton FC via Getty Images)

Tonda Eckert says he received death threats and was told by the police not to drive anymore following the Southampton Spygate scandal.

‌



Southampton were kicked out of the Championship play-off final after admitting they spied on rival clubs. They will start the 2026/27 season on -4 points, while Eckert is still awaiting the outcome of a Football Association charge.

‌



The German coach is at the centre of things, after the FA determined the spying on Oxford United, Ipswich and Middlesbrough was a "contrived and determined plan from the top down".

‌



Saints' hierarchy have stuck by Eckert, who remains in charge despite the possibility he could be handed a lengthy touchline ban. The 33-year-old says he was sent supportive messages from "well-known colleagues" in both England and Germany, but the reaction from the public was intense.

JOIN US ON FACEBOOK! Latest news, analysis and much more on Mirror Football's Facebook page

Asked if he received death threats, Eckert told Kicker: "Yes, it could no longer be handled without the police. I do not want to go into details, only this much: I was advised not to drive myself any more, but to sit in the back of the car instead. That was very difficult."

‌



He added: "It was a situation no coaching course prepares you for. No training explains how to react when, for security reasons, you are suddenly supposed to sit in the back seat. As I said, it was very difficult."

The FA charged Eckert with acting in an improper manner, or bringing the game into disrepute. He has been overseeing pre-season preparations in Germany, with Saints targeting promotion back to the Premier League once more, and admits the charge hanging over his head has complicated things.

"I would be lying if I said that it is not in the back of my mind," Eckert told BBC Radio Solent. "I think that's true for everyone involved, but the positive thing is I just love the game. I love football - there's so much to prepare for.

‌



View 2 Images Tonda Eckert could still be banned for Spygate (Image: Trevor Wilkinson/MI News/NurPhoto via Getty Images)

"There's so many things to do in the pre-season with training preparation and a transfer window, and once you lock into whatever is needed at the very moment, that's all that matters.

"It's not that it's constantly on my mind but obviously we'll be happy when the decision comes at one point and until then I just keep my head down, working, and I think the boys are in a good place."

‌



Eckert has insisted he didn't know the EFL rules banning the observation of opponents' training sessions, which he says is common practice in other countries.

"It's tough to read some of the things that are out there, I've held my hand up for this judgement on something I have authorised," he previously told BBC Radio Solent.

"I am responsible and I apologise for bad judgement; we've be in now for a week and there comes a point to look forward and from the first day back in, there's been lots of smiles and a good energy in the place again."

Sports.content:
Man Utd ready to battle Barcelona for £13.7m star as they establish transfer plan B

Manchester United are looking to make additions at left-back and, should they miss out on Newcastle's Lewis Hall, then they could battle Barcelona for Spanish teenager Jorge Salinas

View 2 Images Man Utd have been keeping tabs on highly rated Spanish teenager Jorge Salinas

Manchester United are reportedly considering a move for Racing Santander full-back Jorge Salinas, who is their back-up option should they miss out on Lewis Hall.

‌



The Newcastle star is on the club's shortlist and the Magpies have already seen a number of their leading lights leave this summer. Bruno Guimaraes is being pursued by Arsenal and could follow Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali out the door with the club into a period of transition.

‌



Eddie Howe has just called time on his five-year tenure and United are looking to seize on the uncertainty around the club by going after Hall, who has continued to blossom since moving to St James' Park from Chelsea.

‌



Newcastle are in no hurry to cash in on Hall and would demand an offer in excess of £50million before they even considered letting the England international leave - which has left United having to look elsewhere.

‌



As it stands the Red Devils are prepared to pay Salinas’ €16m (£13.7m) release clause, but it remains to be seen how willing the player himself is to make the move. Barcelona see Salinas as a replacement for Joao Cancelo, who is set to make the move to Saudi Pro League outfit Al-Hilal.

Chelsea sign Jordan Henderson as ex-Liverpool captain completes shock move

Former Liverpool midfielder Jordan Henderson has completed a move to Chelsea at the age of 36, having been allowed to leave Brentford for nothing midway through his contract

Chelsea have completed a deal to sign England international Jordan Henderson. The former Liverpool captain, 36, has signed a two-year deal at Stamford Bridge after leaving Brentford.

Henderson still had another year left on his contract with the Bees but was allowed to leave for nothing. The addition of the former Liverpool star is intended to add more experience to a young Chelsea squad under Xabi Alonso, with ex-Manchester United and Arsenal forward Danny Welbeck, 35, also arriving on Saturday.

‌



The veteran duo have been joined at Chelsea this summer by the more youthful trio of Morgan Rogers (24), Marco Palestra (21) and Valentin Barco (22).

‌



"Given the size of the club, the manager, who I have great admiration for, and the quality of the players, this was a huge opportunity I couldn’t turn down," Henderson said.

Sports.title: Ex-Premier League star blocks £113m Real Madrid transfer as FIFA receive complaint
Sports.content:
Ex-Premier League star blocks £113m Real Madrid transfer as FIFA receive complaint

Max Gradel, the ex-Bournemouth winger, has filed a complaint to FIFA that has thrown Yan Diomande's reported £113million move to Real Madrid into doubt

View 2 Images Real Madrid have reportedly agreed a deal to sign RB Leipzig star Yan Diomande (Image: (Photo by Stuart Franklin/Getty Images))

Former Premier League winger Max Gradel has filed a compliant to FIFA regarding Yan Diomande's proposed £113million move to Real Madrid.

‌



Diomande, 19, who is viewed as one of the most exciting attacking talents in world football, has agreed a club-record deal to join Jose Mourinho's Madrid side this summer. The Ivory Coast international netted 13 goals and added 10 assists in 36 matches for RB Leipzig last season and appears destined for Los Blancos.

‌



But the transfer has run into a major stumbling block due to a legal dispute over representation rights, according to AS and Defensa Central. Real Madrid struck the deal with Roc Nation, the sports agency founded by rapper and businessman Jay-Z, under the belief they were Diomande's sole representatives.

‌



Liverpool transfer need brutally exposed as Leeds stun Andoni Iraola - 5 talking points READ MORE :

Ex-Man Utd star tipped for bright future by Alex Ferguson speaks out on being clubless READ MORE :

However, Maxidel Management, headed up by ex-Bournemouth, Leeds United and Leicester City forward Gradel, have launched a lawsuit to FIFA alleging a breach of contract. Maxidel brokered Diomande's switch from Leganes to Leipzig last summer and maintain they hold his rights until he departs the German club.

The dispute has brought the deal to a grinding halt, despite Diomande previously being on the verge of putting pen to paper on a five-year contract at the Santiago Bernabeu.

Real Madrid are said to be absolutely furious over the situation, feeling misled by the lack of transparency throughout negotiations. Having reached a broad agreement with Roc Nation, the sudden emergence of Maxidel's claim has thrown serious complications into the mix.

‌



Ivorian journalist Malick Traore shed light on the club's frustrations, saying: "Real Madrid are angry with Diomande's representatives at Roc Nation, after discovering that the player is still tied to a contract with other agents."

View 2 Images Former Premier League star Max Gradel has put a halt on Yan Diomande's move to Real Madrid (Image: Getty Images)

The fury is aimed solely at Roc Nation, not at Diomande himself. Real Madrid now face a precarious predicament, as settling a commission with the incorrect agent could trigger severe sanctions from FIFA.

‌



Gradel, 38, started his senior career at Leicester and made his breakthrough during the Foxes' League One title-winning season in 2008/09, scoring some important goals including an equaliser in a 2-2 draw at MK Dons.

He went on to leave Leicester in 2009 and join Leeds on loan and then on a permanent deal. He played a pivotal role in propelling the Whites to promotion from League One before delivering the standout campaign of his career in the Championship, netting 18 times across 41 appearances.

That impressive spell secured him a transfer to Saint-Etienne in Ligue 1, where he remained for four seasons before heading back to England with a Premier League switch to Bournemouth. Gradel subsequently turned out for Toulouse, Sivasspor and Gaziantep before transitioning into life as a football agent.

Sports.title: Raducanu to miss US Open
Sports.content:
Emma Raducanu's stress fracture will force her to miss the US Open.

The British No 1 suffered the injury to her right lower leg during the grass-court season and made a late decision to pull out of Wimbledon.

According to the Press Association, following consultation with her medical team, Raducanu has concluded she will be unable to play in New York later this month.

While the news comes as no surprise given the nature of the injury and the fact Raducanu has only recently taken her first tentative steps back on court wearing a protective boot, it is another blow to the 23-year-old.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Hours before withdrawing from Wimbledon, Emma Raducanu told the media that she intended to compete despite pushing beyond anything she normally would.

Having made positive progress last summer, including winning her first matches at Flushing Meadows since lifting the trophy five years ago, it has been a frustrating 12 months for Raducanu with more persistent physical issues.

After a foot injury severely hampered her pre-season training, Raducanu then spent two-and-a-half months off court with a post-viral illness after initially falling unwell in early February.

She finally returned for the end of the clay-court season having rehired Andrew Richardson, the coach who guided her to the US Open title, but the pair's time on court together has been limited.

Sports.title: Hearn wants £1m per-year deal for Pollock from Northampton
Sports.content:
England star Henry Pollock is expected to seek a significant pay rise to remain at Northampton after agent Eddie Hearn said he is worth at least £1 million a year.

Pollock's current contract with Saints expires next summer and is thought to pay around £150,000 a year.

Since agreeing that deal in December 2024, the back-row forward has made his international debut, toured with the British and Irish Lions and helped Northampton win the 2025-26 Gallagher Prem title.

"He's certainly a seven-figure player," Hearn told Telegraph Sport.

"The way rugby's going and what Pollock is doing, his value over the next couple of years will skyrocket, and I think the value of rugby will."

Sports.title: Maguire handed Solheim Cup return as Europe's captain's picks revealed
Sports.content:
Leona Maguire has been included among Team Europe's captain's picks for next month's Solheim Cup, with Anna Nordqvist adding three more rookies to her line-up.

Maguire has featured in the last three Solheim Cups, top-scoring as an unbeaten rookie in Europe's away win over Team USA in 2021 before making further appearances in 2023 and 2024.

The 31-year-old was the highest-ranked European player in the Rolex Women's World Golf Rankings not to qualify automatically, having posted three top-10 finishes on the LPGA Tour this season but missed the cut in four of the five majors.

Image: Leona Maguire has won 8.5 points for Team Europe from 12 matches during her three previous appearances

Maguire was the only player with past Solheim Cup experience named among Nordqvist's picks, announced live on Sky Sports, with Spain's Julia Lopez Ramirez, France's Nastasia Nadaud and England's Mimi Rhodes the other selections.

Image: Team Europe's confirmed 12-player line-up for this year's Solheim Cup

"I'm really excited to be part of Team Europe again in September," Maguire said. "I love the Solheim Cup, it brings the best out of my game and I love being part of the team."

It leaves Team Europe with four debutants in their line-up to face Angela Stanford's Team USA at Bernardus Golf in the Netherlands from September 11-13, where the hosts look to regain the trophy after their 2024 loss.

Sports.title: All you need to know about the 2026 Solheim Cup
Sports.content:
Where and when will the next Solheim Cup take place? How does the scoring system work? Which players can qualify? All you need to know about the 2026 edition...

What is the Solheim Cup?

The Solheim Cup is a three-day competition played between teams of 12 players from the USA and Europe.

The event launched in 1990 and was named in honour of Karsten and Louise Solheim and family - the founders of Karsten Manufacturing Corporation, which makes PING golf equipment.

The biggest team tournament in women's golf, where Team USA face Team Europe, is next held from September 11-13, 2026.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ahead of the 2026 edition of the Solheim Cup, watch the greatest shots in the history of the competition

The Solheim Cup is back to even-numbered years to avoid clashing with the Ryder Cup, which moved to odd-numbered years after being postponed in 2020 due to the Covid-19 pandemic.

It resulted in the Solheim Cup taking place in back-to-back years in 2023 and 2024, but now reverts to a biennial contest - like the Ryder Cup - as it was previously.

The tournament heads to the Netherlands for the first time in 2026, with Bernardus Golf - a course previously used for the Dutch Open on the DP World Tour - confirmed as the venue.

Image: Bernardus Golf in Cromvoirt, close to Eindhoven, will host the 2026 Solheim Cup

The Championship course, designed by American golf course architect Kyle Phillips, is described as a heathland golf course with tricky water hazards, a compact layout, an architecturally stunning clubhouse and world-class practice facilities.

The 2028 edition is set to take place at the iconic Valhalla Golf Club in Kentucky, 20 years on from hosting the Ryder Cup, with the host courses for all future contests yet to be announced.

What is the format?

There are 28 matches played over the three days, under three different types of match play - foursomes, fourballs and singles - with each match worth one point to the team total. The team which gets to 14.5 points first will win the Solheim Cup.

There are two sessions of foursomes, each containing four matches of two golfers from Europe competing against a pair from the USA. Team members alternate between shots and each team uses one ball.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look back at some classic winning moments from down the years between Team USA and Team Europe at the Solheim Cup

Fourballs also sees two golfers from each team compete but each player uses their own ball, with the lowest score from each pair counting towards their total in that match.

All players compete in the Sunday singles, where every member from the USA team plays against a European opponent in a head-to-head contest.

Who has qualified for Team Europe?

The European qualification period for the Solheim Cup began at the 2024 La Sella Open and ended following the conclusion of the 2026 AIG Women's Open, played at Royal Lytham & St Annes, on August 2.

The top two players on the Ladies European Tour Solheim Cup points list and the next available six via the world rankings secured their spots.

Charley Hull topped the LET Solheim Cup points list to secure her an eighth consecutive Solheim Cup appearance, while Esther Henseleit pipped Chiara Tamburlini to second by 0.9 points after her runner-up finish at the final women's major of the year.

England's Lottie Woad will make her debut as the highest-ranked European in the world rankings, having won on the Ladies European Tour and LPGA Tour over the past 13 months since turning professional.

Sweden's Maja Stark and Linn Grant return for their third consecutive Solheim Cups, with France's Celine Boutier, Spain's Carlota Ciganda and Denmark's Nanna Koerstz Madsen the others to qualify automatically.

Image: Team Europe's automatic Solheim Cup qualifiers

Captain Anna Nordqvist announced Ireland's Leona Maguire as one of her four wild card picks, along with three debutants: Spain's Julia Lopez Ramirez, France's Nastasia Nadaud and England's Mimi Rhodes.

The top seven players on the Solheim Cup list at the end of the qualifying period, based on points accumulated from all ranking events, will secure automatic qualification for Team USA.

The next top two players on the Rolex Women's World Golf Rankings at the end of the qualifying period - not already qualified - will also earn a spot, while the captain will have three picks to complete her line-up.

Angel Yin and Jennifer Kupcho have already scored enough points to definitely be in the top seven on the Solheim Cup list, leaving 10 more qualification spots available.

The qualification campaign began at the 2024 FM Championship and will end following the 2026 CPKC Women's Open, from August 20-23, where the nine automatic qualifiers will be confirmed.

Anna Nordqvist has been named as Europe's captain for 2026, having made nine consecutive appearances as a player and served a dual role as vice-captain for the last two contests.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Take a look back at the best of Charley Hull's seven Solheim Cup appearances for Team Europe

The Swede succeeds Suzann Pettersen, who was captain for back-to-back editions in 2023 and 2024, with Nordqvist choosing Caroline Hedwall and Mel Reid as her vice-captains for the 2026 edition of the contest.

Hedwall has represented Europe as a player on five occasions, with Reid competing four times and also acting as vice-captain in 2019 and 2024.

Angela Stanford has been named as Stacy Lewis' successor and will captain Team USA for their Solheim Cup title defence in the Netherlands.

Stanford featured six times for Team USA and was part of three winning teams, with her last appearance seeing her part of a comeback victory on European soil in 2015.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Team USA Solheim Cup captain Stacy Lewis described the stress of watching the Sunday singles of their 2024 victory

The former major champion has been an assistant captain for the last three editions of the biennial contest, including to Lewis for each of the previous two contests.

The 47-year-old has so far announced Kristy McPherson and Paula Creamer as vice-captains. She added five-time Solheim Cup player Brittany Lang as an assistant captain on June 3.

Who has previously won the Solheim Cup?

Lewis' side took a 10-6 advantage into the Sunday singles at Robert Trent Jones Golf Club, leaving them requiring just 4.5 points for victory, with Megan Khang, Allisen Corpuz and Rose Zhang all posting big wins to move them closer to their target.

Celine Boutier and Leona Maguire won their matches to move Europe closer to the 14 points required to win for the fourth time in a row, only for Lilia Vu to secure the half-point needed for victory when she won her final two holes to tie against rookie Albane Valenzuela.

Sports.title: Celtic learn CL opponents as Brighton discover European route
Sports.content:
Celtic will play Austrian champions LASK for a place in the league phase of the Champions League, while Brighton will face CFR Cluj or Tromso in the Conference League play-off round.

The draws for the Champions League, Europa League and Conference League play-offs were made on Monday, with Rangers, Hearts, Hibernian, Motherwell and Larne also learning their qualifying routes.

Martin O'Neill's Celtic will host the first leg of their tie against LASK on August 18 or 19, with the return fixture on August 25 or 26. The losers of the tie will drop into the league phase of the Europa League.

Brighton, who finished eighth in the Premier League last season, will play Romanian side CFR Cluj or Norwegian club Tromso to decide who will reach the Conference League's league phase.

The tie will be played on August 20 and 27, with Brighton hosting the second leg, either side of their opening game of the season at home to Aston Villa on August 23, live on Sky Sports.

Rangers and Hearts learn Europa League routes

Rangers and Hearts discovered their Europa League play-off opponents, should they win their third-round qualifying ties.

Derek McInnes' Rangers side travel to Poland this week to face Jagiellonia Bialystok on Thursday in the first leg, with the second leg next week.

Should they win, they will play Northern Irish champions Larne or Iberia 1999 of Georgia in the play-offs. The first leg on August 20 would be at Ibrox, with the return tie the following week.

If Larne lose, they will move into the Conference League play-offs and play Lincoln Red Imps or Omonia.

Image: Derek McInnes is searching for his first victory as Rangers manager

Hearts, who dropped into the Europa League after their Champions League exit, have been drawn against AGF Aarhus of Denmark or Sabah of Azerbaijan in the play-off round.

The first leg of that tie would be at Tynecastle Park on August 20, with the return tie on August 27.

However, Wouter Vrancken's side must first get past Benfica in the third-round qualifying tie. They are away in Portugal on Thursday and back at home next week.

Both clubs will be guaranteed another chance at qualifying for a European competition this season, with the Conference League play-off round awaiting if they lose in the third round of the Europa League.

Rangers would play Jablonec or RFS while Hearts would be up against Paide or SK Rapid.

That has resulted in both clubs requesting that their league game between the first and second legs of any potential play-off tie be postponed, meaning Rangers' game against St Mirren and Hearts' trip to Falkirk are both to be rearranged.

Motherwell and Hibs discover Conference League fate

Motherwell will play Bundesliga club Freiburg - last season's Europa League finalists - in the Conference League play-off round if they beat HJK Helsinki.

Alfred Johansson's side visit HJK on Wednesday in the third qualifying round, with the second leg at Fir Park on Thursday August 13.

Hibernian will play IFK Gothenburg or Gent in the Conference League play-off round should they get past KF Shkendija.

Hibs host Shkendija on Thursday with the second leg on August 13 for a place in the play-offs.

The Conference League play-offs take place on August 20 and 27.

Sports.title: Can Mount be the third midfielder Man Utd are looking for?
Sports.content:
"Why go out searching for a midfielder when you've got Mason Mount at home?"

…A perhaps uncomfortable conversation for most Manchester United supporters to have, but that's the question Mount is forcing Michael Carrick and the Carrington training staff to consider.

The 27-year-old has started every game in pre-season for United and has been among their standout performers against Wrexham, Rosenborg and Atletico Madrid.

"It's only pre-season" will be a valid rebuttal for anyone looking to jump on the Mount hype train. Preparations ahead of the new season can often provide a false representation of reality given differences in fitness and the lack of any real competitive edge. Most United fans will be familiar with this testing assessment of performances during this period.

Andreas Pereira, now plying his trade in Brazil, was once dubbed the "pre-season Pirlo" for his assured performances ahead of new seasons. Those same performances failed to emerge come the beginning of the regular campaign.

Putting that to one side, though, what pre-season does offer is an insight into a manager's thinking. And as United fans wait eagerly to discover what Carrick's side will look like ahead of his first full season in charge, Mount's role could be telling.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Speaking in April, Mason Mount revealed his goal of bringing the Premier League back to Old Trafford

The former Chelsea man has slotted seamlessly into a deeper role. His composure on the ball and industry as a No 8 is exactly what United will be looking for in the market. United prioritised a midfield overhaul this summer following the departure of Casemiro and two signings have already been made in that area.

Andrey Santos from Chelsea has already made an impression on fans and United await to see what impact Youri Tielemans can have. However, fully fit ahead of the new campaign, pre-season has provided Mount with an opportunity to pin down a role and it's one he's very much taking.

While he appears a revelation, Mount's deployment deep in a midfield two isn't new under Carrick. Nor is it new for Mount, having played roughly 4,500 mins as a No 8 or No 6 and 7,000 behind the front man.

Image: Mason Mount percentage by position since 2019/20 (2023/24 excluded due to minimal minutes)

Mount started United's final game of last season, a win at Brighton, in that very role alongside Kobbie Mainoo. While there was no obvious defensive-minded midfielder between the two, the pair's technical ability allowed them to dominate Brighton's midfield in a comprehensive display.

The Brighton game was United's first taste of life post-Casemiro, and Carrick's immediate solution was to play Mount. However, another occasion Carrick chose Mainoo and Mount behind Bruno Fernandes was during a 0-0 draw against Sunderland towards the back end of the season, which was less successful. United were lucky to escape the Stadium of Light with a point.

While Casemiro represented a more combative option that United now lack, Carrick has expressed his admiration for Paris Saint-Germain's midfield dynamic in the past and could be eyeing the chance to replicate those relationships at Old Trafford.

At Parc des Princes, on-the-ball mastery is king over industry and tough tackling and it's a core that's been game-changing for the back-to-back Champions League winners. Mount, whose attitude has seemingly allowed him to adapt to many sides, seems prime for that evolution.

Throughout his career, Mount has always emerged as a managerial favourite. It happened under Frank Lampard on loan at Derby County and back at Chelsea. Thomas Tuchel also found a place for Mount in his teams, while Erik ten Hag was eager to bring him to Old Trafford in a deal worth up to £60m and hand him the famed No 7.

That decision still mystifies most onlookers, as, at times, has the transfer in general. However, before even a ball was kicked under Ruben Amorim following Ten Hag's sacking, he was quick to express his "love" for Mount.

Mount seems to have it all going for him, with coaching staff and team-mates alike evidently willing him on to find success as he enters his third season at United. But anyone familiar with Mount will know the issue doesn't solely lie with his role or ability. Mount's issue has been his fitness, and it's plagued him throughout his Old Trafford career.

Since joining United, Mount has missed around 70 matches with injury and has spent 394 days sidelined. But without hoping to tempt fate, there are signs that he can establish himself as a useful tool in United's squad.

With a return to Champions League football awaiting Carrick's side and a desire to avoid the domestic cup disasters of last season, there will be ample chance for Mount to be deployed. Three years on, United may just be getting the midfielder they hoped they'd signed.

Is he like a new signing? Not really, but United do have Mount at home.

Sports.title: USA cricketer Akhilesh Reddy given eight-year ban under anti-corruption code
Sports.content:
USA cricketer Bodugum Akhilesh Reddy has been banned from all cricket for eight years by the ICC after being found guilty of three counts of breaking anti-corruption rules by a tribunal.

Akhilesh Reddy, who has been banned from cricket since November awaiting the hearing, was found guilty of charges relating to match-fixing, soliciting others to fix matches, and destroying evidence that could have been relevant to the investigation.

The ICC says the offences took place during the Abu Dhabi T10 competition.

"USA player Bodugum Akhilesh Reddy has been banned from all cricket for eight years after an ICC Anti-Corruption Tribunal found him guilty of breaching three counts of the ICC Anti-Corruption Code," the ICC said in a statement.

"The charges relate to the Abu Dhabi T10 2025 in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) for which the ICC was appointed by the Emirates Cricket Board (ECB) as the Designated Anti-Corruption Official (DACO).

"The ban is backdated to 21 November 2025, when Reddy was provisionally suspended.

"The Tribunal found Mr Reddy guilty of the following offences under the Code:

"Article 2.1.1 - Attempting to fix, contrive or otherwise influence improperly, or being party to an agreement or effort to fix or contrive in any way or otherwise influence improperly, the result, progress, conduct or other aspect of matches in the ADT10 2025.

"Article 2.1.4 - soliciting, inducing, enticing, instructing, persuading, encouraging or intentionally facilitating (or attempting to do the former) another participant to breach Article 2.1.1 of the Code in one or more matches in the ADT10 2025.

"Article 2.4.7 - Obstructing the DACO's investigation through deletion of data and messages from a mobile device which may have been relevant to the DACO's investigation."

Sports.title: English FA to drop support for Gianni Infantino after Wales withdraw backing
Sports.content:
The Football Association will formally withdraw its support for Gianni Infantino’s re-election as the Fifa president, adding to the mounting pressure on his crisis-hit tenure. In a significant development, the FA will write to Fifa confirming it no longer backs Infantino for a fourth term in charge, having previously offered its endorsement. Their move comes after the Welsh FA dropped its backing for Infantino’s candidature.

More European countries are expected to follow suit in an attempt to force his resignation. The Football Association of Finland became the first country to withdraw its support last week.

The Guardian reported on Sunday that Uefa federations have been preparing a mass withdrawal of letters supporting Infantino. All bar five of the continent’s 55 member associations had communicated their backing before last week’s revelation of his privately backed plan to sell a stake in the World Cup.

The FA has previously fallen into line behind Infantino, who will helm an extraordinary Fifa congress confirming the UK’s hosting of the 2035 Women’s World Cup in November if he is still in position. But it has been consistent in condemning his doomed Fifa Forward Enterprise scheme, publicly and in private representations. On Saturday, it called for a “full and robust review of Fifa’s leadership and governance”, and its latest move is a further escalation.

While the FA’s stance is robust, it is not expected to publicise its withdrawal letter due to a view, also held in some other parts of Europe, that the movement to unseat Infantino needs to gather momentum on different continents. Opposition within Europe will not be difficult to achieve, but Infantino’s future may hinge on the degree of leadership taken by members of the Asian Football Confederation and Concacaf, where opinion on his reign has been more divided.

The Football Association of Wales confirmed on Monday morning that it no longer supports Infantino. “The Football Association of Wales hereby confirms its withdrawal of support for the candidature of Mr Gianni Infantino, for re-election as Fifa president for the 2027–2031 term,” it said.

“The recent failures in good governance, processes, leadership, values, stakeholder management, communications and sound judgment have led us to a position where Mr Infantino has lost the confidence of the FAW to remain at the helm of world football. Failing to put the best interests of football first is a failure we cannot accept.”

Welsh football and its representatives have played a key role in moves to oppose Infantino. In a meeting of member associations last Thursday, Laura McAllister, a Uefa vice-president and former Wales international, advocated a Europe-led boycott of Fifa competitions if Infantino did not scrap the FFE scheme. It led to a collective agreement that effectively rendered the plan untenable.

Sports.title: Vinícius Júnior to Arsenal doesn’t make sense. That’s why it may work | Jonathan Wilson
Sports.content:
Sometimes what is needed is something different.

There is a long history in football of counterintuitive thinking being successful, of the benefits of creative tension, of adding grit to the oyster to generate the pearl, but even so, the news that talks between Vinícius Júnior and Arsenal on personal terms are progressing comes as something of a shock. Mikel Arteta’s great followers of a blueprint adding a free spirit like the Brazilian? Really?

Vinícius returns to Real Madrid this week after the World Cup with movement on his future expected relatively soon. He has 12 months remaining on his contract and Madrid are keen either to tie him down to a new deal or to sell him while he will attract at least some kind of fee. As their squad rebuild goes on under José Mourinho, Madrid’s position is readily understandable. They have already signed Bernardo Silva, Denzel Dumfries, Marc Cucurella and Ibrahima Konaté this summer; removing Vinícius’s £420,000 a week (about $30m/year) basic wages significantly increases their financial headroom.

There’s been a sense since Kylian Mbappé joined Madrid two years ago that having him and Vinícius together left the squad unbalanced. Why would you need two rapid forwards who both prefer to cut in from the left, particularly when Rodrygo, who tended to be consigned to the right before tearing his ACL in March, would also prefer to play from the left? Yan Diomandé is likely to confirm his move to Real Madrid from RB Leipzig this week. Although the Ivorian has said he would rather play on the right, he too has spent much of his career on the left.

More broadly, Vinícius does not seem a natural Mourinho player. His pace and technical excellence are undoubted, but he has never been the most diligent at fulfilling his defensive responsibilities. Mourinho likes a forward who can improvise, and worked successfully with Cristiano Ronaldo at Madrid, but it’s difficult to see how he could indulge more than one such player at a time, and Mbappé will take precedence.

But those concerns about tracking, about the willingness to stick to a gameplan, about the capacity to retain possession are just as relevant to Arteta as they are to Mourinho – arguably more so, as Arteta believes far more in structured attacking planning than Mourinho. Is Vinícius, after years of freedom at Madrid, really going to accept those rigid structures?

It’s been fairly clear since the second half of last season that Arsenal would be looking to strengthen their left side. The sale of Leandro Trossard to Beşiktaş did not come as a huge surprise. The 31-year-old is reliable and played a valuable role last season, starting 21 of the 38 league games and coming off the bench on a further 10 occasions, but there is not much stardust about him. Gabriel Martinelli started 11 league games and came off the bench 19 times, and his pace can be a great asset, but it’s no longer clear that he is at his best on the left. The signing of Eberechi Eze last summer looked like an attempt to add creativity from that flank but his tendency to drift infield when Arteta needs his left-sided forward to stay wide meant that by the end of the season he tended to be used centrally behind a striker.

Vinícius would give Arsenal greater attacking thrust. At his best, under Carlo Ancelotti, he could transform a game in seconds. His pace, dribbling ability and finishing mean that no matter how stale a game seems to have gone, no matter how under pressure his team may be, they are never more than seven or eight seconds from a potential goal. It’s easy to see why Arsenal are tempted by him. He would immediately be their highest-profile player, adding a sense of direction to a summer that, at least from a recruitment point of view, has seemed to be drifting. Arsenal missed out on Morgan Rogers, who joined Chelsea, while Julián Álvarez, who would seem a much more natural fit on the Arsenal left, appears more likely to go to Barcelona, if sufficient financial levers can be pulled.

But the fact Vinícius is not a natural fit may be part of the attraction. It was, after all, the season after signing Erling Haaland, far from a typical Pep Guardiola player, that Manchester City won the treble. A player who does not quite fit, who kicks against the general philosophy, can make a process team less predictable. The friction can produce valuable sparks.

Haaland, it’s fair to say, is a different personality from Vinícius and, as a center-forward, there was never a worry he was going to leave his full-back exposed. Vinícius is a bigger risk. He would certainly be an expensive one, not just in terms of his own salary but the inflationary pressure that could have on wages at the club more generally.

But he would also add a dash Arsenal have lacked that would make the accusation of being dead-ball plodders hard to sustain. And with Trossard gone, there is a left-sided hole that needs filling.

Sports.title: Newcastle reject first bid from Arsenal for captain Bruno Guimarães
Sports.content:
Arsenal have stepped up their attempt to sign Bruno Guimarães by finally beginning formal transfer negotiations and making an opening offer, which Newcastle have rejected.

Guimarães met Newcastle’s incoming manager, Matthias Jaissle, for the first time on Monday at the team’s pre-season training camp at La Manga after a post-World Cup holiday in Brazil.

There had been suggestions that the 28-year-old midfielder would fly to London for a medical at Arsenal, but instead he boarded a commercial flight to Spain. Once at La Manga, he was expected to tell Jaissle of his determination to swap Tyneside for north London, but everything hinges on whether Arsenal are prepared to meet Newcastle’s valuation for a player with two years remaining on his contract.

While executives at Arsenal believe Guimarães is worth a maximum of £70m – and a bid in that ballpark was rejected on Monday – Newcastle value their captain at around £80m.

If some sort of compromise seems likely given Arsenal – negotiating, initially, through intermediaries – have spent much of this summer in pursuit of a midfielder at the top of Mikel Arteta’s shopping list, Newcastle are under no pressure to sell.

Indeed, having sold Anthony Gordon and Sandro Tonali to Barcelona and Tottenham respectively this summer, they would prefer to offer Jaissle the benefit of Guimarães’s talent and experience as he rebuilds the squad.

The 38-year-old was believed to be keen to assess the Brazilian’s mindset as begins preparations for the opening Premier League match at home to Liverpool two weeks on Sunday. Although the former Al-Ahli and RB Salzburg manager is still to be officially confirmed as Howe’s successor, Jaissle has been with his new squad since arriving in southern Spain on Saturday. Newcastle are waiting for the completion of some final paperwork before formalising his appointment.

View image in fullscreen Guimarães has had several battles with Arsenal over the past few seasons. Photograph: Scott Heppell/Reuters

One signing completed by Newcastle on Monday involved Lukas Hornicek’s £26m move from Braga. The 24-year-old Czechia goalkeeper is expected to replace Nick Pope as the team’s first choice, with Pope now likely to leave.

Hornicek caught Newcastle’s eye after seven clean sheets during Braga’s run to the Europa League semi-finals last season. At 6ft 6in, he cuts an imposing figure in goal and has been highly praised for the sort of high-calibre footwork that should improve Newcastle’s ability to play out from the back.

Hull had hoped to recruit Hornicek, but he turned down a move to the promoted club last month.

Sports.title: Marc Skinner may have been a Marmite manager but Manchester United’s budget was spread thin | Tom Garry
Sports.content:
“If we want to compete at this later stage, we’ve seen what we’ve got to do, as a club. It’s our choice now, isn’t it? We have to look at what we seriously want to achieve … It takes, sometimes, a punch in the face to wake up.”

Those were the words of the Manchester United head coach Marc Skinner after his side went out of the Women’s Champions League with elimination by Bayern Munich in April. Just over four months later, the bruise from that punch has faded, but so, it would seem, have the club’s ambitions to compete in the transfer market, and Skinner has decided not to get into the ring for another round.

The 43-year-old wanted that run to the quarter-finals to trigger further investment in the starting team. The club, though, feel that the levels of spending in the transfer market are unsustainable and therefore want to focus on developing young, homegrown talent. Once that juxtaposition was firmly established this summer, it was inevitable that Skinner and United were likely to part company, as they did on Monday, to end his five years in charge.

United’s Marmite manager, Skinner certainly divided opinion in the WSL. He was the league’s longest-serving manager by a distance, but arguably also the most heavily maligned coach online. In the sport, though, there are coaches who admire the job he did on – according to the most recent set of WSL clubs’ financial accounts – a little over a third of the playing budget of Chelsea and around half that of Arsenal’s.

For members of the media, Skinner’s press conferences will probably be one of the most memorable aspects of his tenure, unique because of the extensive length of the former Birmingham and Orlando head coach’s answers. For example, before the 2025 Women’s FA Cup final, one of his answers was 1,000 words long.

View image in fullscreen Marc Skinner instructs his players in a Champions League tie against Brann in September 2025. Photograph: Craig Brough/Action Images/Reuters

To some, his determination to provide long, considered responses was a sign of his thoughtfulness and showed an admirable desire to be transparent. To others, his drawn-out answers demonstrated an inability to be concise and this communication problem dogged his relationship with the fans throughout much of his tenure. Often, unintentionally, his words would irritate sections of the fanbase. In 2025, one former United player privately described Skinner as a “great bloke, but he goes on a bit” and it is fair to say not every player liked his team-talk style, while others enjoyed his passion.

On the pitch, the 2022-23 season, Skinner’s second, was the club’s strongest as they finished second in the table, boosted by a robust defensive record, conceding 12 times in 22 games, and they came within a whisker of winning the title. Then there was the comparatively low moment of languishing down in fifth in the 2024-25 campaign, counteracted by winning 2025’s Women’s FA Cup, lifting United’s first major women’s trophy.

Yet, whether you loved him or loathed him at Leigh Sports Village, Skinner overachieved at United on a purely pound-for-pound basis, reaching four domestic cup finals – including three consecutive Women’s FA Cup finals – despite typically operating on a mid-table budget for much of his incumbency. He was certainly not every player’s cup of tea, and there will be lessons he will need to learn from the highs and lows of his five years at the club, but now that both of the coaches who have managed United’s women in the modern era have wanted to leave, in part, because of funding issues, there are questions for the club’s hierarchy to answer.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Weekly Sign up to Moving the Goalposts No topic is too small or too big for us to cover as we deliver a twice-weekly roundup of the wonderful world of women’s football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

In the 2024-25 season, of the eight WSL clubs to publish their wage bills via Companies House, United’s ranked fourth for expenditure, and it was a similar story in 2023-24. For next season, they will operate on a far smaller wage bill than the big-spending independent club London City Lionesses and there are understood to be fears held among some staff at United that they are soon likely to be outbid for players’ wages by Tottenham too.

The club embarked on new direction this summer, establishing a long-term aim to sustainably succeed with young homegrown players and play exciting football in line with what they believe are the traditions of the club and their culture. Yet that seems to be at odds with the targets outlined during the 2024-25 season when their “Project 150” included a “Mission 1” for the women to win a first WSL title by the club’s 150th anniversary in 2028.

Whoever comes in as the club’s head coach – and an appointment is likely to happen quickly, with background checks having already been carried out on candidates – they will need to be prepared to work with youngsters and develop them rather than trying to sign established, international stars. They will also have to accept that key first-team players – such as Melvine Malard who was sold to Chelsea this summer – may well be poached by a rival.

Sports.title: On the spot: 50 of the most famous – and infamous – Panenka penalties of all time
Sports.content:
It is 50 years since Antonin Panenka won the European Championship for Czechoslovakia with the most audacious penalty ever taken. His signature chip wasn’t instantly eponymous. A search of the British newspaper archives shows that it was barely mentioned until Francesco Totti dusted it off for the internet generation at Euro 2000.

It was at least another decade before Panenka was commonly used as a noun, and it did not have its own Wikipedia page until 2014, but in 2026 every football fan has an idea of what it means. The 50th anniversary is the perfect time to remember 50 of the most famous – and infamous – attempts.

A Panenka is in the eye of the beholder. Ben Lyttleton, doyen of penalties and author of the superb Twelve Yards, asked the man himself what constituted a true Panenka. Their criteria is strict, based on the line of the ball, its trajectory and where it hits the net. But that disqualifies, among others, Zinedine Zidane in the 2006 World Cup final (“This penalty is the obvious misuse of the Panenka classification!”), so we’ve used a looser definition. If the ball was kissed rather than kicked, the penalty is eligible. Rob Smyth

View image in fullscreen The man himself, pictured earlier this year. Photograph: Björn Steinz/The Guardian

Antonin Panenka, 1976

Czechoslovakia 2-2 West Germany (5-3 pens)

This one needs no introduction. RS

Antonin Panenka, 1979

Czechoslovakia 2-0 France

The next high-profile Panenka came almost three years after Belgrade, when he fooled the France keeper Dominique Dropsy with a sensual chip in a vital European Championship qualifier. Czechoslovakia ultimately pipped an emerging France – Michel Platini et al – and finished third at Euro 80. RS

Diego Maradona, 1984

Napoli training

Most of Diego Maradona’s penalties were high-wire acts, Panenkas in spirit, with the ball pointedly passed nowhere near the corner to ensure maximum vaccination. We can’t find any examples of him taking an actual Panenka in a professional game, so we’re including one he took in training at Napoli. Two reasons: one, it’s Maradona; and two, the arc of his penalty shouldn’t be possible. But then we’d already seen him do it in open play. RS

Eric Cantona, 1989

Bordeaux 1-1 Beauvais (3-4 pens)

In February 1989, Eric Cantona was famed more for attitude than ability, having served bans for a tackle of comic-book violence, insulting the France coach, and greeting a friendly substitution by blootering the ball into crowd and tossing his shirt. So Marseille loaned him to Bordeaux and, when a cup game against lower-division Beauvais went to penalties, he went last. Juggling his way to the spot, he tried a Panenka, but the effort held up in the wind before landing in a puddle, allowing the keeper, who’d gone the wrong way, to wander over and pick it up, confirming the upset. Daniel Harris

Gianluca Vialli, 1990

Monaco 2-2 Sampdoria

In the 20th century, certainly in England, a Panenka was generally referred to as a “cheeky chip”. It was also a favourite of a cheeky chap. Gianluca Vialli scored several for Sampdoria, often under extreme pressure: against Genoa in the Scudetto-winning season of 1990-91, and twice during Samp’s Cup Winners’ Cup triumph of 1989-90. The first was against Borussia Dortmund in the last 16, the second in the first leg of the semi-final against Arsène Wenger’s Monaco. Vialli scored two goals in four minutes that night, then two in three when Sampdoria beat Anderlecht 2-0 in the final. RS

Michal Bilek, 1990

Czechoslovakia 5-1 USA

It’s neat that another Czech player was the first to try a Panenka at a World Cup, even if the circumstances were completely different. Czechoslovakia were 4-1 up in a group game against the USA when Michal Bilek, who had already scored one orthodox penalty, tried to pay tribute to 1976. He fluffed it. After making a simple save, the USA keeper Tony Meola barked: “Get that shit outta here!” RS

Gary Lineker, 1992

Nottingham Forest 1-1 Tottenham

Nobody ever talks about the Panenkas that Gary Lineker scored. There were at least three for Tottenham, and we’re pretty sure he’s the first serial Panenka-er in English football. The first completed a hat-trick on live TV – a big deal back in 1990 – and led to a brief post-match discussion in which only one of Elton Welsby and Glenn Hoddle knew about the Euro 76 final. Lineker also scored “a nifty little Panenka”, as he put it, in a Rumbelows Cup semi-final against Nottingham Forest. This one was particularly sweet – the keeper was Mark Crossley, a penalty-saving expert who had denied Lineker from the spot in the previous season’s FA Cup final. RS

Gary Lineker, 1992

England 1-1 Brazil

A kick remembered for comedic reasons, largely through Micah Richards and Alan Shearer chuckling about it every few months on their podcast. But at the time this was a moment of pathos and heartbreak, as Lineker passed up his best, if not his last, chance to equal Bobby Charlton’s all-time England goal record. Jonathan Liew

View image in fullscreen With a share of England’s goalscoring record for the taking, Gary Lineker dinks tamely into the arms of the Brazil goalkeeper Carlos. Illustration: Mark Leech/Offside/Getty Images

Eric Cantona, 1994

Manchester United 1-1 Newcastle United (5-6 pens)

In May 1994, Eric Cantona was untouchable, having inspired Manchester United to a league title then a double. In the FA Cup final, he’d gently rolled two penalties into the same corner of the net, Chelsea’s Dmitri Kharine diving the wrong way as if compelled by the shamanic power of Gallic flair. But in a shootout against Newcastle at that summer’s illustrious Ibrox International Challenge Trophy, the success of his previous Panenka in 1989 persuaded him to try another. Pavel Srnicek obligingly dived out of the way only for the kick to sail over the bar as United lost 6-5. DH

Djalminha, 1995

Guarani 2-1 Internacional

Brazil’s Djalminha, the maverick’s maverick, is best remembered for his signature rainbow flick, so it’s no surprise he was partial to a rainbow kick from the penalty spot. The first of many was scored against Sergio Goycoechea, whose elastic penalty saves had taken Argentina to the final of Italia 90. “I noticed that he always jumped early and committed to a corner,” said Djalminha, “so I thought that was the moment to try the chip.” It quickly became tried and trusted. RS

Dwight Yorke, 1996

Sheffield United 0-1 Aston Villa

Dwight Yorke was so sick of Mark Bosnich saving his penalties in training, he tried something completely different. It worked, so he promised to do it for real the next time Aston Villa were given a spot-kick. That was met with ridicule, but Yorke was true to his word and settled an FA Cup tie at Bramall Lane with a goal that changed his life. “Suddenly,” said Yorke in Born to Score, “the football world was very aware of this cheeky young buck who had dared to execute such an outrageous spot-kick. I definitely detected an increased interest in me after that match.” RS

Gianluca Vialli, 1996

Chelsea 2-4 Wimbledon

There’s no Internet Panenka Database (IPDb), which makes it impossible to say categorically who did what when. But Vialli’s consolation Panenka, at the end of a game in which Chelsea were thrashed by a rampant Wimbledon, may be the first of the Premier League era. Neil Sullivan, who had been beaten from the halfway line by a very different kind of chip earlier in the season, came tantalisingly close to saving it. RS

Dwight Yorke, 1998

Aston Villa 1-0 Arsenal

“If the penalty taker has the bottle to do that, good luck to him,” said David Seaman, who was Panenka-ed on the last day of the 1997-98 season. “There isn’t much a goalie can do except look pretty stupid when it goes in.” Or hold their position, which Seaman did when Yorke took another penalty against him nine months later in an epic league match between Manchester United and Arsenal. His bluff called, Yorke sidefooted wide. RS

John Eyre, 1999

Torquay 0-1 Hull City

If only there was a transcript of the great Neville Southall’s internal monologue as this piece of effrontery floated gently past him. RS

Francesco Totti, 2000

Netherlands 0-0 Italy (1-3 pens)

In their Euro 2000 semi-final with the co-hosts, Italy put on a defensive masterclass while down to 10 men. In the inevitable shootout, Frank de Boer was denied by Francesco Toldo and Jaap Stam blasted his kick into orbit. Stam was immediately followed by Francesco Totti, whose falling leaf penalty foxed Edwin van der Sar and had the Dutch lurching towards despair. It also introduced the Panenka to a new generation. John Brewin

View image in fullscreen Francesco Totti brings the Panenka into the 21st century. Illustration: Henri Szwarc/Bongarts/Getty Images

Mixu Paatelainen, 2001

Hibernian 0-0 Hearts

A last-minute penalty to win an Edinburgh derby is the stuff of dreams – and nightmares. Mixu Paatelainen only took it because Hibs’ usual taker, Russell Latapy, had gone awol two days earlier. After scoring a hat-trick against Hearts earlier in the season, Paatelainen probably thought he could do anything. As his chipped effort sailed over the bar, he was disabused of the notion. RS

Thierry Henry, 2003

Arsenal 3-2 Newcastle

Five days after the Battle of Old Trafford, Arsenal kickstarted their Invincible season with a ding-dong win over Bobby Robson’s Newcastle. The winner was teased softly down the middle by Henry. Maybe it was an unspoken message of defiance that Arsenal would continue to do things their own way. Maybe it meant nothing. Or maybe he was just trolling Ruud van Nistelrooy. RS

View image in fullscreen Thierry Henry went full va-va-voom for his winning penalty against Newcastle. Illustration: Jamie McDonald/Getty Images

Mickaël Landreau, 2004

Nantes 1-1 Sochaux (4-5 pens)

For all the spot-kicks these keepers face, surely they’d understand the right and wrong way to disguise a Panenka. Not poor Mickaël Landreau. He had the chance to secure the 2004 Coupe de la Ligue final for Nantes, but his headlong dash failed to give his lob the requisite power. Sochaux ultimately flipped the result and won the cup. Jeff Rueter

Liam Lawrence, 2004

Huddersfield 0-0 Mansfield (4-1 pens)

Liam Lawrence scored 12 penalties, one short of Francis Lee’s English league record, to help Mansfield to the Third Division playoff final in 2003-04. When that game wheezed to a penalty competition, Lawrence was standing on the halfway line with his teammate Bobby Hassell (“a proper angry little fella”). On the Under the Cosh podcast, Lawrence remembered their exchange.

double quotation mark LL I’m gonna dink it. BH No you’re not. LL I am, honestly. I’m gonna dink it down t’middle. He’s gonna dive; there’s no way he’s gonna stand there in a playoff final. BH Liam, don’t you fuckin’ dink that ball.

He dinked that ball against the bar – “I got too much juice in my run-up” – to leave Mansfield 2-0 down after two penalties. “By the way,” Lawrence added, “the keeper did dive.” RS

Helder Postiga, 2004

Portugal 2-2 England (6-5 pens)

Helder Postiga was a typical Tottenham signing of the era: a talent unfulfilled, sold at a loss after a single Premier League goal. His revenge on English football was to equalise in normal time of the Euro 2004 quarter-final and then send David James stumbling with Portugal’s sixth penalty, a kick so under-amped it barely scraped over the line. Then Darius Vassell missed, the Portugal keeper Ricardo scored, and a tournament that England’s golden generation could have won had slipped from their grasp. JB

Peter Crouch, 2006

England 6-0 Jamaica

The then-Liverpool striker scored an England hat-trick as part of World Cup preparations, yet many only remember him lifting the ball well over the bar from 12 yards. Arrogance certainly played its part, wanting to secure his treble in style, but he had to wait, earning the ire of the usually calm Sven-Göran Eriksson. “It was a golden opportunity to practise for a penalty shootout, but he made a joke out of it,” the head coach spewed. “He’s apologised.” Will Unwin

View image in fullscreen Judging by his expression, Peter Crouch knew he’d got his penalty wrong as soon as he hit it. Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty Images

Artem Milevskiy, 2006

Ukraine 0-0 Switzerland (3-0 pens)

You’re excused if you don’t remember this one: it came after 120 minutes of the most soporific football ever played. RS

Zinedine Zidane, 2006

Italy 1-1 France (5-3 pens)

The nerve to do it in a World Cup final. The scene was nothing new for Zidane. He’d already bagged that brace eight years earlier against Brazil; it had to be him, in his last game, dinking it off the crossbar, past Gianluigi Buffon. It was going to be the dream sendoff – until Marco Materazzi and the anger took over. Taha Hashim

View image in fullscreen Zinedine Zidane steps up… Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

View image in fullscreen … and beats Gianluigi Buffon all ends up. Photograph: Nick Potts/PA Archive/PA Images

Yann Kermogant, 2010

Cardiff 2-3 Leicester (agg: 3-3; 4-3 pens)

To miss a Panenka is to embrace infamy. To do so in a Championship playoff is to be consumed by notoriety. In a shootout, with the decisive kick? Insanity. Kermogant, a useful French striker who found his home in England’s second tier, dollied his kick into the body of the grateful Cardiff keeper, David Marshall. Kermogant is remembered for this moment above all others, possibly for eternity. He even has his own Bonnie Tyler adaptation. JB

Sebastián Abreu, 2010

Uruguay 1-1 Ghana (4-2 pens)

If we were picking a Panenka XI, Sebastián Abreu would be one of the first names on the team sheet, so it’s apt that he administered one at a World Cup. A tumultuous quarter-final, best remembered for Luis Suárez’s handball and Asamoah Gyan missing a penalty in the last minute of extra-time, ended with the softest of executions. RS

Andrea Pirlo, 2012

England 0-0 Italy (2-4 pens)

When England somehow prolonged their Euro 2012 quarter-final against Italy to penalties, and with his team leading 2-1 after two goes each, Joe Hart bounced and laughed, seeking to put Andrea Pirlo off … then plunged towards the corner as the ball wafted gently above him and in. “He felt I was too charged not to dive,” Hart reflected on a mood-switching moment. England missed their next two kicks, with two Italian successes finishing them off. “I saw [Hart] making strange movements, so I hit it like that,” Pirlo confirmed afterwards. DH

View image in fullscreen Andrea Pirlo icily dinks his penalty over a fired-up Joe Hart. Illustration: Matthias Schräder/AP

Sergio Ramos, 2012

Spain 0-0 Portugal (4-2 pens)

For such a tactile defender, Sergio Ramos was surprisingly partial to a tender Panenka. His most important came in the Euro 2012 semi-final against Portugal. Bruno Alves missed Portugal’s next kick and Spain went on to demolish Italy in the final. RS

Maicosuel, 2012

Udinese 1-1 Braga (agg: 2-2; 4-5 pens)

The one that cost €20m. Maicosuel had just joined Udinese from Botafogo when his Panenka was saved in a Champions League playoff against Braga. It was the only miss of the shootout. Udinese, coached by Francesco Guidolin, dropped into the Europa League and the big payday went to Braga. “I still can’t get it out of my head,” said Guidolin six years later. “It stalks me.” RS

Graziano Pellè, 2012

SC Heerenveen 2-2 Feyenoord (6-7 pens)

Sudden death, the last 16 of the cup. You’re the seventh-choice penalty-taker, you have to score or it’s over, and you have the chutzpah to try a Pellènka? RS

Rogério Ceni, 2013

São Paulo 0-0 Corinthians (3-4 pens)

No surprise that one of the great goalscoring keepers should beat his opposite number with a Panenka. His reaction after scoring in this Campeonato Paulista semi-final shootout carried a simple message: it’s not personal, it’s strictly business. His São Paulo team lost anyway; Ceni thought he had kept them alive with a save from Alexandre Pato, but he was fractionally off his line. Pato scored the retake emphatically. RS

Alexandre Pato, 2013

Gremio 0-0 Corinthians (3-2 pens)

Five months later, Pato had to score to keep Corinthians in their Copa do Brasil quarter-final against Grêmio. It was an inopportune time to take one of the worst Panenkas ever seen. RS

Alexis Sánchez, 2015

Chile 0-0 Argentina (4-1 pens)

It’s impossible to top the historic significance of the definitive Panenka, but Alexis Sánchez came closer than anyone. His swaggering penalty, which barely left the ground, won Chile their first Copa América – and unlike Czechoslovakia in 1976, they were the hosts. The playful nature of Sánchez’s winning moment only added to the nationwide euphoria. RS

Aaron Ramsey, 2017

Serbia 1-1 Wales

The Wales team of Gareth Bale, Aaron Ramsey and co regularly made history. In a World Cup qualifier in 2017, Ramsey unwittingly did so by scoring a Panenka at the same end of the same ground in Belgrade where it all began. “I didn’t know,” he said, “but that is quite a nice touch.” In more ways than one. RS

View image in fullscreen Aaron Ramsey does a Panenka more completely than most. Photograph: Peter Cziborra/Reuters

George Calintaru, 2017

Juventus Bucuresti 1-2 Steaua Bucuresti

A Panenka can seriously damage your health. When George Calintaru fluffed the chance to equalise for newly-promoted Juventus Bucuresti against Steaua with the last kick of the game, his teammates set upon him in frustration. He then punched a table in the dressing room and broke a finger. RS

Fedor Smolov, 2018

Russia 2-2 Croatia (3-4 pens)

Russia’s shock run to the 2018 World Cup quarter-final was soundtracked by raucous support. The crowd in Sochi met the occasion as a shootout with Croatia was all that stood between them and a semi-final. Pedants may contend that Fedor Smolov’s opening attempt lacked enough lob to qualify as a Panenka, but his tame prod up the middle made Danijel Subasic’s job easy to open the sequence in Croatia’s favour. JR

Lionel Messi, 2020

Barcelona 2-2 Atlético Madrid

If you’re going to bring up 700 career goals in an empty stadium, you might as well do it in style. RS

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi’s penalty record is suprisingly human, but he got the one that gave him his 700th goal right. Photograph: David Ramos/Getty Images

Fara Williams, 2020

Reading 3-1 Aston Villa

This unusual penalty from Fara Williams might not satisfy the Panenka purists. But we’ve included it because it captures a recurring sub-genre: an all-time-great using the Panenka as an expression of undeniable superiority. RS

Ademola Lookman, 2020

West Ham 1-0 Fulham

During his time at Fulham, Ademola Lookman attempted a Panenka against West Ham with the last kick of the game but his feeble chip landed straight in the arms of Lukasz Fabianski. “I’m disappointed and angry,” said his manager Scott Parker in a rare moment of post-match honesty. “You can’t take penalties like that and he knows that.” Yara El-Shaboury

Santi Cazorla, 2021

Al-Gharafa 0-2 Al Sadd

Not many players score orthodox penalties with their left and right feet, never mind Panenkas. Santi Cazorla is a member of the latter club – right foot against Newcastle in 2014, left foot against Al-Gharafa in 2021. RS

Sergio Agüero, 2021

Man City 1-2 Chelsea

City were set to secure the Premier League title but, in front of zero fans during Covid, Sergio Agüero did not feel the pressure. He decided to chip down the middle; Édouard Mendy almost fell for it but had enough time to get up and claim the ball. Chelsea went on to win, and Agüero issued a public apology. WU

View image in fullscreen Sergio Agüero’s Panenka attempt almost, but crucially only almost, fools Édouard Mendy. Photograph: Shaun Botterill/AFP/Getty Images

Marta, 2022

France 2-1 Brazil

Birthday gifts can be a pain to give, especially when the celebrant seems to have given themself the perfect present. Such was life if Marta was on your gift-giving list in 2022, with the Brazilian legend opening that day’s friendly against France in sublime fashion.JR

Karim Benzema, 2022

Manchester City 4-3 Real Madrid

A moment of mischief at the end of a pulsating and painfully serious match. Eight days later, Benzema scored a more orthodox penalty to put Madrid into another Champions League final. RS

View image in fullscreen Real Madrid’s improbable run to winning the 2022 Champions League included Karim Benzema coming up clutch – again. Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The Guardian

Achraf Hakimi, 2022

Morocco 0-0 Spain (3-0 pens)

If you’re going to put your country into their first World Cup quarter-final, you might as well do it in style. RS

Gaëtane Thiney, 2023

Real Madrid 0-1 Paris FC

We can’t say for sure that this is the first Panenka in the Women’s Champions League, but it’s definitely the first to knock Real Madrid out of the competition. RS

Antoine Mille, 2024

Les Herbiers 2-2 Châteauroux (3-4 pens)

In which the Les Herbiers goalkeeper Téo Hamelin is so affronted that, after saving one of the more pitiful Panenkas ever taken, he flings the ball straight back at the unfortunate Mille. RS

Marta, 2025

Orlando Pride 2-1 San Diego Wave

If you have already missed your penalty, but opponents’ encroachment has given you a second chance, just how bold do you have to be to attempt a Panenka from the retake? That’s what Marta did in the NWSL for Orlando Pride in 2025, chipping in off the underside of the crossbar to secure a 2-1 victory over San Diego Wave, and remind everybody of her ageless class and skill. Tom Garry

Alexia Putellas, 2025

Roma 0-4 Barcelona

Even the greats fluff their efforts sometimes. Alexia Putellas, one of the best women’s footballers of all time, clipped a Panenka harmlessly over the crossbar during a Champions League victory for Barcelona when her team were only 1-0 up. She redeemed herself from the spot later in the match – that time, tucking safely into the bottom corner. TG

Tiaguinho, 2025

Brazil U17 0-0 Paraguay U17 (5-4 pens)

A Panenka is a dish best served cold. RS

Brahim Díaz, 2026

Morocco 3-0* Senegal

Brahim Díaz had the chance to become a Moroccan hero when he won and then took a stoppage-time penalty that could have ended his country’s 50-year trophy wait. Instead, after a 16-minute delay caused by Senegal’s protests, his Panenka was easily caught by Édouard Mendy. “He had a lot of time before taking the penalty, which must have disturbed him,” said the Morocco manager Walid Regragui. No kidding. Then again … YE-S

View image in fullscreen Brahim Díaz’s miss saw Morocco squander their chance to win the Afcon. Or so we thought… Photograph: Paul Ellis/AFP/Getty Images

Mohamed Salah, 2026

Australia 1-1 Egypt (2-4 pens)

Sixty-one penalties were taken at the 2026 World Cup. The surprise is that Mo Salah’s Panenka for Egypt in their shootout against Australia was the only one. Fifty years after it came straight outta leftfield, the Panenka is now firmly part of the mainstream. RS

Sports.title: ‘They are terrified’: Como spark row with fans over controversial new stadium policy
Sports.content:
Como, the surprise package of last season’s Serie A, who qualified for the Champions League for the first time, will revoke season tickets from fans who fail to attend four home matches, under a series of new rules that have sparked a row among supporters.

The club, coached by the former Arsenal midfielder Cesc Fàbregas, said on Monday that supporters “who miss more than three home matches without what it considers a valid reason risk having their season tickets revoked”. Another new rule bans fans from wearing the opposing team’s shirts or scarves anywhere in the stadium except the away section.

“Demand for tickets far exceeds supply and, for that reason, I asked the club to find ways to ensure tickets for the [Giuseppe Sinigaglia stadium] end up in the hands of genuine Como supporters – those who want to be there to back the team,” the chair, Mirwan Suwarso, said in a lengthy statement on Instagram.

“There have been too many occasions when away fans have celebrated inside our home sections, while Como supporters, who would have proudly backed the team, were unable to get a ticket.”

On the ban on wearing rival teams’ shirts, scarves and other symbols outside the away end, the club said the measure was introduced for safety reasons. “Our aim is to make the Sinigaglia the true home of our fans and a fortress for our team,” said Suwarso. “We want to ensure the Sinigaglia remains a place where grandparents feel comfortable bringing their grandchildren, where families can enjoy football together, and where passion never crosses the line into disrespect.”

On social media, many criticised the measures as overly harsh, arguing that work commitments, health issues or family responsibilities can prevent people from attending matches without making them any less loyal to the club.

La Provincia, Como’s local newspaper, said its newsroom had received dozens of calls and emails from concerned supporters. “Some worried about health problems or being unable to attend because of bad weather, as well as people who frequently travel for work,” the newspaper wrote. “They are terrified and all asking the same question: will our season tickets be taken away?”

Italy’s national newspaper, Corriere della Sera, reporting reactions from supporters on social media, quoted one fan asking: “Do we need to be accompanied by our parents when we hand in our excuse, like at school?”
