World.title: “For safe and strong Georgia”: Saturday march in Tbilisi. Georgia protests video blog
World.content:
612th day of protests in Tbilisi

“For a Safe and Strong Georgia” was the main slogan of the traditional pro-European Saturday march held in Tbilisi on 1 August 2026.

Before the march began, participants observed a minute’s silence in memory of a teenager who was recently killed in central Tbilisi and who would have turned 18 today.

Hundreds of people gathered once again in Avlabari Square for the 612th consecutive day of protests. With construction work continuing on Rustaveli Avenue, the march followed an alternative route for the second Saturday in a row, starting at Avlabari metro station and ending outside the parliament building.

For more than a year and half – since November 2024 – continuous protests have been taking place in Georgia, with demonstrators demanding that the country return to the path of European integration. Every evening thousands, and often tens of thousands, gather in Tbilisi and several other cities. Over this time dozens of participants have been detained, many have faced criminal charges, and some have been sentenced to prison terms. For the first time in the history of independent Georgia, the country has up to 150 prisoners of conscience, including women. Among them is Mzia Amaglobeli, founder of the popular outlets Batumelebi and Netgazeti. In 2025 she was sentenced to two years in prison for slapping a police officer. Protesters demand the release of all political prisoners, new parliamentary elections – as they do not recognize the results of the 2024 vote – and the repeal of all anti-democratic laws adopted over the past two years. To suppress the protests, the ruling Georgian Dream party has increasingly tightened repression against civil society and the media. However, protests in various forms continue.

612th day of protests in Tbilisi

World.title: South Ossetia presidential election: Meet the seven contenders
World.content:
Presidential contenders in South Ossetia

Registration of candidates for South Ossetia‘s snap presidential election, scheduled for 18 September 2026, has closed, with seven contenders set to run.

Yet, even before the campaign has begun, many in South Ossetia believe the outcome is already decided. Most see acting President Marat Kambolov – a senior Russian official appointed from Moscow – as the clear frontrunner and the likely winner.

Candidates

Marat Kambolov

The initiative groups have nominated acting President and Prime Minister Marat Kambolov, former KGB officer Kazbek Kodoyev, and Eduard Gabarayev, a member of the extra-parliamentary Iron party and a former defence ministry official.

***

Murat Valiyev

Several political parties have also nominated their own candidates. Khoh Chochiyev, a former State Protection Service officer, has been nominated by the extra-parliamentary Iry Farn party. Another security official, Murat Valiyev – a serving officer in the presidential State Protection Service and a former KGB officer – has been nominated by the Patriots of Alania party.

***

Zurab Kokoyev, chairman of the Unity party, which has previously been in power, has also announced his intention to run, despite having earlier backed Kambolov’s nomination.

***

Fatima Khugayeva

Finally, the only woman in the race and a newcomer to South Ossetian politics is Fatima Khugayeva, a retired lieutenant colonel in Russia’s Interior Ministry – making her yet another candidate with a security background.

She has been nominated by the Development Party. Although she was born in Moscow, Khugayeva has South Ossetian roots. After retiring, she returned to her ancestral homeland, got married, and now works as a deputy headteacher while teaching history.

Dropouts

In a surprise development, Georgiy Kabisov, leader of the Iron party, a former head of the Information and Press Committee who previously served a prison sentence for fraud, abandoned his earlier plans to run for president. His party now appears set to throw its full support behind its other nominee, Eduard Gabarayev. Vladimir Kelekhsayev, leader of the Unity of the People party and a former member of parliament, has also decided not to run. His party is likely to back one of the remaining contenders.

Following the close of registration, the Central Election Commission will review the documents submitted by the registered contenders to ensure they meet all legal requirements. Only then will they officially acquire candidate status, allowing them to open campaign accounts and begin collecting signatures. Some contenders may still be eliminated at this stage if irregularities are found in their paperwork.

Frontrunner, ‘supporting cast’ and ‘independent players‘

Of the seven contenders, only Prime Minister Marat Kambolov appears to have a realistic chance of winning. A Moscow official dispatched from the Kremlin just a few months ago, he has no prior ties to South Ossetia but enjoys unprecedented political backing. Even the territory’s main opposition forces have effectively thrown their support behind him, opting not to contest the election so as not to stand in his way.

Zurab Kokoyev

Kazbek Kodoyev

Most of the remaining candidates are viewed by analysts as technical candidates whose role is largely to fill out the ballot rather than mount a serious challenge.

This includes Kazbek Kodoyev and Zurab Kokoyev.

***

Murat Valiyev is a political newcomer whom the Patriots of Alania party appears to have nominated primarily to give him electoral experience. The campaign will also provide the party, founded only in 2023, with an opportunity to raise its profile. At the same time, the party’s chairman, Dzambolat Tedeyev, has urged voters to back Marat Kambolov.

Khoh Chochiyev

Analysts regard Khoh Chochiyev and Eduard Gabarayev as the more independent contenders.

Eduard Gabarayev

In this context, “independent” means that neither politician is regarded as a technical candidate or as someone willing to run merely to benefit the frontrunner. However, both are backed by different groups of current and former officials, as well as opposition figures.

***

Fatima Khugayeva, meanwhile, is widely seen as a candidate backed by local business interests. The Development Party, which nominated her, is led by businessman and restaurateur Albert Valiyev, who is friends with Khugayeva’s husband, a producer of alcoholic beverages.

However, Khugayeva is not merely being put forward because of her husband’s connections. She has political experience of her own: she remains a member of the Russian party Communists of Russia and has frequently taken part in protest rallies.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

World.title: Russian woman faces prison after calling Armenians ‘rat-like’ people
World.content:
Russian calls Armenians ‘rats’

A criminal case has been opened in Armenia against Russian national Nadezhda Pirozhkova. A blogger who has lived in Armenia for the past year and a half, Pirozhkova came under fire after criticising Vardavar, the Armenian tradition of pouring water over one another on the holiday. She described the custom as an act of aggression. In another video, she referred to Armenians as a “rat-like people”.

Armenia’s Investigative Committee has initiated criminal proceedings against Pirozhkova under the article on “public statements aimed at inciting hatred and discrimination through the use of the internet”. Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for a prison sentence of up to four years under this article. If Pirozhkova is found guilty in court, she could therefore face imprisonment.

For now, however, she has been banned from leaving her place of residence as a preventive measure. The blogger may leave Yerevan only with written permission from a prosecutor or a judge.

Vardavar is one of the principal feasts of the Armenian Apostolic Church, celebrating the Transfiguration of Jesus Christ, although its origins date back to pagan times. It is virtually impossible to stay dry on the streets that day, but taking offence is not customary, as drenching someone with water is considered a way of congratulating them on the holiday. The water is believed to bring health, good fortune and purification.

Pirozhkova’s Instagram posts sparked outrage among social media users—not only Armenians, but also fellow Russians.

Many have not only criticised Pirozhkova but have also called on law enforcement authorities to punish her as severely as possible or deport her from the country.

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian did not rule out the possibility that certain actors interested in damaging Armenia’s image as a tourist destination were behind the spread of such videos. He pointed to the large number of Russian tourists visiting Armenia. In the first half of 2026 alone, Armenia received 1.042 million foreign visitors, around 40% of whom were from Russia.

“It’s interesting, isn’t it? On the one hand, the Russian government imposes trade restrictions [on imports of Armenian products and goods], while on the other, Russians happily travel to Armenia, enjoying its nature, its people and, why not, its traditions,” Yerkanian said.

What else Pirozhkova said

In a video about Vardavar, the Russian blogger said that the holiday made her want to leave Yerevan more than anything else. She described the tradition of pouring water over one another as “the height of tactlessness”. In her view, Armenians do not understand the concept of “personal boundaries” and routinely violate them.

Pirozhkova argued that splashing passers-by with water was disrespectful towards those who did not wish to take part in the celebration.

“If I’m in your country, I’m not obliged to follow your traditions. This is a direct manifestation of aggression.“

Following the video, Pirozhkova has periodically posted about the wave of online abuse directed at her. She has also publicly apologised several times, saying:

“I understand that many people saw it as disrespect towards the Armenian people. And I’m truly sorry. That was never my intention, and it still isn’t.”

At the same time, the blogger has acknowledged that she is using the controversy to promote her Instagram page.

“People recognise me now. Why shouldn’t I make use of something I’ve been through after putting in so much effort? I’ve worked hard for this. Why shouldn’t a person take advantage of circumstances and situations they have rightfully earned? I just want to change my life.“

Foreign nationals are required to respect Armenia’s national customs and traditions

The legal status of foreign nationals in Armenia is governed by the Law on Foreigners. Article 5 of the law states that foreigners in Armenia enjoy the same rights, freedoms and obligations as Armenian citizens. At the same time, it stipulates that “foreigners in the Republic of Armenia are obliged to respect the Constitution and laws of the Republic of Armenia, other legal acts, as well as national customs and traditions.”

The same article also provides that foreign nationals bear the same legal responsibility as Armenian citizens while in Armenia.

Armenia’s Criminal Code provides for penalties for “public statements aimed at inciting or promoting hatred, discrimination, intolerance or hostility against an individual or group of persons on the grounds of race, nationality or ethnicity, as well as the dissemination of materials or objects for that purpose.”

The available penalties include fines, community service, restriction of liberty and imprisonment.

Under Article 329, offences committed “through publicly displayed works, the mass media, or information and communication technologies” are punishable by one to four years’ imprisonment

Commentary

Political commentator Artyom Yerkanian said in an interview with a local television channel::

“After the Russian blogger publicly apologised, this story could have ended there. But some social media users continued calling on the Armenian law enforcement authorities to examine Nadezhda Pirozhkova’s actions and determine whether they amounted to a criminal offence. The authorities decided to respond to those calls.

Perhaps there was no need to be so severe. The court will, of course, take all mitigating circumstances into account.

Perhaps we should not politicise everything. It is obvious that the aim was not to incite ethnic hatred but simply to increase her audience through provocative videos.

In two weeks, the video attracted more than 250,000 views and over 5,000 comments. As a result, the number of followers on her page increased more than fifteen-fold.

In other words, this blogger simply found a ridiculous and foolish way to grow her audience.

Nevertheless, perhaps such cases should be monitored more closely, because this is not an isolated incident.

In recent weeks, there have been several similar cases in which foreign bloggers, particularly Russians, have made remarks discrediting Armenians and damaging Armenia’s reputation as a tourist destination.

There was one case in which a young woman accused an Armenian taxi driver of attempting to rape her. I also recall another similar incident, and there are probably many more. But what is more important?

Notably, these videos are deliberately amplified by non-existent users. An army of fake accounts is spreading this material in pursuit of a specific objective.

It cannot be ruled out that certain forces are behind these fake accounts and are interested in ensuring that Armenia is not perceived as a safe destination for tourists.

Every tourist who enjoys visiting the country indirectly becomes its ‘agent of influence’. Perhaps that is exactly what some people dislike.

I don’t know whether it is a coincidence, but it was precisely during those days that the Russian Foreign Ministry added Armenia to its list of countries where Russians cannot feel safe, citing the possibility that the Armenian authorities could extradite them to third countries. Perhaps it is a coincidence—or perhaps it is not.”

Social media reaction

“If, after a year and a half of living in Armenia, she still allows herself to speak like this, it cannot be dismissed as an accident or naivety.”

“The police should investigate her actions. She’s a planted agent.”

“She should be fined heavily and deported.”

“She should be tried and deported from our country. It’s a matter of the nation’s dignity.”

“If an Armenian had behaved like this in Russia, he would already have disappeared.”

“Foreign visitors are obliged to obey the law, respect the country and its people, and behave like guests.”

World.title: Meet Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver: Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo. Video
World.content:
Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver are young pine martens and the newest residents of Tbilisi Zoo. A local resident found the orphaned cubs alone in an attic and took them home after discovering they had no mother.



However, pine martens are wild predators with powerful teeth and strong natural instincts. Once the cubs had grown up, releasing them back into the wild was no longer an option. Contact with humans had altered their natural behaviour, leaving them unable to survive on their own. Their rescuer therefore turned to Tbilisi Zoo for help.

Konstantin Pkhakadze, head of the zoo’s exotic animals department, said the pine martens arrived at Tbilisi Zoo about a month ago. He said such cases are quite common. People often assume that young animals found alone have been orphaned and need rescuing, but that is not always the case.

In most instances, the mother is nearby, hunting, searching for food or moving her young to a new location. Pkhakadze said intervening at that stage is the biggest mistake people can make. They should not even approach the cubs, as the mother may detect the scent of humans, see it as a threat and never return to her offspring.

Tbilisi Zoo currently has very limited capacity to take in new animals. Its existing site is overcrowded, while most of its resources are being directed towards the construction of a new zoo.

Nitsa, Elvis and Oliver were initially housed in the zoo’s exotics pavilion. However, the small enclosed space was unsuitable for such active and energetic animals. Zoo staff therefore built a temporary outdoor enclosure, giving the pine martens more space, fresh air and room to move freely.

Tbilisi Zoo‘s history spans nearly a century. It was founded on 10 February 1927 on the basis of the Caucasian Society for the Acclimatisation of Animals, which had been keeping wild animals since the early 20th century, though without official zoo status. The zoo was originally built on 70 hectares in the Vere River gorge. Over the years, the expansion of the capital — and later the devastating flood of 13 June 2015 — significantly reduced the territory of the old zoo. Today, it covers five hectares and is home to around 1,500 animals, each with its own story. In this video series, we will introduce you to the residents of Tbilisi Zoo. We will show how their day unfolds, how they interact with other animals and people, and how their behaviour changes depending on the weather and the season. Get ready to hear many fascinating stories.

Pine martens at Tbilisi Zoo

World.title: Georgia’s opposition launches campaign to restore voting rights for emigrants
World.content:
In Georgia, the opposition alliance Coalition for Change and the Strategy Aghmashenebeli party have launched the Emigrant’s Vote campaign, calling for the restoration of Georgian citizens’ right to vote from abroad in parliamentary and municipal elections.

Under the new Election Code, approved by the ruling Georgian Dream party on 17 December 2025, emigrants are no longer allowed to vote from abroad. Instead, they must travel to Georgia to cast their ballots.

One of Coalition for Change’s members, Tengo Tevzadze, announced the launch of the campaign, saying the initiative would culminate in a constitutional challenge seeking to restore emigrants’ right to take part in elections.

According to Tevzadze, the campaign aims to demonstrate that allowing emigrants to vote is consistent with Georgia’s constitution and that every Georgian citizen, regardless of where they live, should be able to take part in elections.

Tevzadze noted that Georgian Dream won just 13.4% of the overseas vote in the disputed 2024 parliamentary election, which the opposition says was rigged. He argued that this was why the authorities later moved to strip emigrants of their voting rights.

Tevzadze argues that depriving emigrants of the right to vote violates Georgia’s constitution and is unfair to a group of citizens that makes a significant contribution to the country’s economy.

The campaign’s organisers have set out two main demands: restoring emigrants’ right to vote and creating an electoral system that allows Georgian citizens living abroad to cast their ballots.

“We need as many emigrants as possible to sign the petition so that, alongside political efforts, we can also challenge the regime through legal means. Through a constitutional lawsuit, we will clearly demonstrate that emigrants’ participation in elections and their voting rights are protected by the constitution, and that Georgians, both at home and abroad, must be able to take part in free and fair elections,” Tengo Tevzadze said.

Voting rights for Georgian emigrants

World.title: Evening illuminations in South Ossetia: Video
World.content:
Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

Major reconstruction work has been completed in the South Ossetian capital, Tskhinval. The city centre has been renovated, dozens of streets repaired, and new utility networks installed.

The redevelopment of Theatre Square included new lighting, benches and marble planters, while boxwood and juniper shrubs were planted. Several school and college buildings, along with the Kosta Khetagurov State Drama Theatre, have also been restored.

The work was funded through Russia’s investment programme.

The terminology, place names and views expressed in this article are those of the author and do not necessarily reflect the editorial position of this website.

Evening illuminations in South Ossetia

World.title: Russian mass strike on Ukraine leaves several dead and dozens injured. Video from Lviv
World.content:
Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

Russia launched a mass overnight attack on Ukraine on 30 July, according to Ukrainian authorities, firing a total of 74 missiles and 284 attack drones. Ukraine said its air defences intercepted a significant number of the incoming targets, but some missiles and drones struck their intended targets.

Several regions across Ukraine came under attack, including Lviv, Kyiv and the Dnipropetrovsk region.

In Lviv, one resident was killed. In the village of Radushne, near Kryvyi Rih, a ballistic missile struck the home of a large family. Six people were killed, including three children, while several others were injured.

Lviv Mayor Andriy Sadovyi said the city had suffered direct Russian missile strikes on residential buildings for the first time in a long period.

The heaviest damage was reported on Paton and Vyhovskoho streets, where more than 20 residential buildings, a school, two kindergartens and other civilian infrastructure were damaged.

Rescue workers recovered the body of a man from beneath the rubble.

According to the latest official figures, 34 people, including three children, were injured in the attack on Lviv. Nine people were rescued from damaged buildings. Emergency crews are continuing search and rescue operations and clearing the debris.

Lviv city authorities said some residents whose homes were damaged would be provided with temporary accommodation, while municipal services are assisting those left homeless.

Russian strike on Ukraine: Video from Lviv

World.title: Russian anti-war politician posts from Paris after 'foreign agent' accusation
World.content:
Russian anti-war politician Boris Nadezhdin said he had left the country, weeks after Moscow designated him a "foreign agent" and disqualified him from running in a parliamentary election.

Standing in front of the Eiffel Tower in Paris, Mr Nadezhdin posted a video to his Telegram channel on Monday.

"Hi everyone! I have some good news. I’m alive and free. Unfortunately, I’m not in Russia at the moment," he said.

"Right now, I need to get my bearings and figure out what to do next. I’ll write about my plans later."

Mr Nadezhdin, 63, a former liberal politician has been an outspoken critic of Moscow's war in Ukraine but — like some other critics — had tried to work within the rules of Russia's tightly controlled political system to be able to continue to voice his views publicly.

His departure marks the loss of yet another prominent opposition voice willing to challenge the Kremlin from inside Russia, with most critics of President Vladimir Putin now either in jail or in exile.

His hopes of running for parliament in September were squashed when the justice ministry added him on July 10 to its "foreign agents" list — a label widely applied by the authorities to people they deem to be engaged in anti-Russian activity with alleged backing from abroad.

The following week, he was questioned by police and received a small fine in court for displaying "extremist symbols" on social media, a charge he described as ridiculous.

Russian politician Boris Nadezhdin, accused of displaying "extremist symbols," attends a court session in the town of Dolgoprudny outside Moscow, Russia, Friday, July 17, 2026. (AP: Pavel Bednyakov)

Mr Nadezhdin said the authorities were "silencing me, forcing me out of politics and making my life extremely difficult".

Russia has clamped down hard on dissent since going to war in Ukraine in 2022.

Pro-Kremlin politicians accuse the West of trying to destabilise Russia and say some censorship is necessary to safeguard national unity while Moscow is locked in an existential struggle with Ukraine and the West.

Mr Nadezhdin attempted to mount a run against Mr Putin for the presidency in 2024 but was disqualified on technical grounds by the Election Commission.

Reuters

World.title: Myanmar releases rare images of ousted leader Aung San Suu Kyi
World.content:
The son of Myanmar's detained former leader Aung San Suu Kyi said a visit by a delegate of the International Committee of the Red Cross was the first positive development concerning her in more than five years.

"This may be a first step, but it must not be the last," Kim Aris said in a statement, adding he has not yet received independent confirmation of his mother's condition or wellbeing.

The meeting was the first publicised visit between her and a foreign official since she was ousted in a 2021 coup.

The military deposed Suu Kyi in February 2021, jailing the Nobel Peace Prize laureate and triggering an ongoing civil war that has killed more than 100,000 people, according to monitor ACLED.

The coup leader and former junta chief, Min Aung Hlaing, was installed as civilian president in April following highly restricted elections.

The images could not be verified by AFP but artificial intelligence tools found no instances of fabrication. (Reuters: Myanmar Government spokesperson/Handout)

Suu Kyi, now 81, was moved to house arrest later that month after Min Aung Hlaing said he had commuted the rest of her sentence.

She was detained on a host of charges that rights groups say were confected to sideline her and her popular National League for Democracy party.

The president's office said in a statement that Arnaud de Baecque, the Resident Representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) to Myanmar, met with Suu Kyi on Monday morning, local time.

Suu Kyi is seen shaking hands with a man who appears to be de Baecque in a photo released by the president's office.

Another image shows Suu Kyi cutting a birthday cake, and another shows the cake with text reading: "Happy Birthday Aunty Suu."

ASEAN's big risk of engaging with Myanmar's junta For engagement to actually work, ASEAN needs to treat all sides in Myanmar fairly, not just the generals.

The images could not be verified by AFP but artificial intelligence tools found no instances of fabrication, and no versions of the images were found online before Monday.

AFP has contacted the ICRC for comment.

"We are happy to see her photo like this if it's really her meeting with the ICRC," a veteran politician of her party told AFP on condition of anonymity.

"We can know now that she's alive.

"However, Aunty should be released immediately as she's being detained unlawfully."

Suu Kyi being used as 'bargaining chip'

Authorities have not disclosed the exact location of Suu Kyi's detention in the capital Naypyidaw, nor how many years of her sentence remain.

Her son, Kim Aris, a British national, has sought independently verified proof that his mother is alive after she was transferred to house arrest.

Aung San Suu Kyi's son, Kim Aris, has fought for the release of his mother for years. (ABC News: Imogen Cook)

The 11-nation Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) has excluded member state Myanmar's leadership from high-level summits since the coup.

However, neighbour Thailand has been leading an effort to bring Myanmar back in the diplomatic fold, both bilaterally and through the regional bloc.

Min Aung Hlaing has travelled to India, China and ASEAN member Laos since his change in position, and he is scheduled to make an official visit to Thailand this week.

"It's the old military game plan to use Suu Kyi as a bargaining chip," independent Myanmar analyst David Mathieson told AFP.

Some ASEAN nations have long called for proof of life, Mr Mathieson said, adding the timing of the government-permitted meeting between Suu Kyi and the ICRC representative — days before Min Aung Hlaing's trip to Bangkok — was no coincidence.

"As a gesture to the international community, it's the wildcard Min Aung Hlaing was holding close to his chest," he said.

Aung San Suu Kyi pictured for first time in years Myanmar's detained former president Aung San Suu Kyi has been moved from prison to house arrest, according to state media.

The Myanmar government could "gain a lot from ASEAN" by permitting access to Suu Kyi, said researcher Morgan Michaels of the International Institute for Strategic Studies.

"Releasing her in particular would go a long way to facilitating Myanmar's re-invitation at the political level," Michaels said.

The continued detention of Suu Kyi remains a major sticking point for some despite Myanmar's recent diplomatic outreach.

ASEAN has pressed for its special envoy to meet Suu Kyi, but Myanmar has so far refused.

Reuters/AFP

World.title: Canberra private school boys ranked female students
World.content:
A prestigious Canberra private school is investigating after male students created a list ranking the appearance of female students and shared it on a year level group chat.

The head of Canberra Grammar School, Justin Garrick, sent an email to staff and parents of students in the affected year level last month informing them that "demeaning commentary" had been circulating among the cohort.

The ABC has chosen not to name the year level.

An email from the head of Canberra Grammar School said the school had not written to students about the list because the incident was still being investigated. (ABC News: Ian Cutmore)

"I am writing to parents and staff only — not students — because we are still investigating," Mr Garrick said in the email on 24 July, adding that the school was taking the matter "very seriously".

The ABC has obtained a heavily redacted copy of the list, which contains 100 names.

It includes a colour-coded ranking system and scores of "S" to "F".

The ranking system is understood to be derived from a grading system in which the highest tier "S" means "superb" or "super" and sits above the traditional "A" to "F" grading system.

A redacted image allegedly showing content sent by Canberra Grammar School students in which they "ranked" the appearance of females. (Supplied)

Concerned families contacted school

In a second email sent to families last Wednesday, also seen by the ABC, the school said it had been contacted by families since news of the list emerged.

"We appreciate the honest and thoughtful conversations we have had over the past few days, as well as the support and understanding shown by our parent community while we have worked through this situation," the email said.

Support for young people and families The Butterfly Foundation: National helpline 1800 ED HOPE (1800 33 4673), 8am-midnight (AEST/AEDT), 7 days a week

ReachOut Australia: Confidential online peer support for young people and online resources for wellbeing

Headspace: Centres in each state and territory or check out eheadspace for online support

The Kids Helpline: 24-hour support on 1800 55 1800

Lifeline: 24-hour support for all Australians on 13 11 14

"Supporting young people through complex matters requires time, sensitivity and care, and we have been mindful of this throughout our response."

The school met with students from the affected cohort last Wednesday to offer support, including from the school's psychologist and chaplain.

"Our intention is to acknowledge that this situation has had an impact on many within the year group, to reinforce the importance of respect and dignity for all members of our community, and to encourage students to consider how they can work together positively as the cohort moves forward," the email said.

Canberra Grammar School has been contacted for comment.

Canberra Grammar's secondary school started accepting female students in 2017. (Supplied: Canberra Grammar School)

Canberra Grammar School has been operating since 1929, and started out with just 50 male students.

In 2017, it began accepting female students.

Canberra Girls Grammar School operates separately, and accepts only female students.

The Canberra Grammar School Parents and Friends Association declined to comment, as did Canberra Girls Grammar School.

World.title: 'Lot of nonsense': Dearden clears air on Cowboys future
World.content:
North Queensland co-captain Tom Dearden has cleared the air about his future and given the club a boost as he targets returning from injury to inspire a finals run.

At the end of the 2023 season Dearden, 26, signed a five-year contract extension through to the end of 2029.

But multiple reports in recent weeks linked him to an early exit for personal reasons due to his pregnant partner, Millie Over, living in Sydney.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

Dearden fronted the media to refute the reports due to the impact they were having on his personal life.

"There's been a fair bit of speculation getting around at the moment. There's been a lot of suggestions that I wanted to move or leave the club," Dearden said.

"That's not the case at all. I don't feel like I should have to get up here and explain myself against speculation.

"It's just been a whole lot of nonsense. I've got my private life with a partner who's pregnant and I'd like for that all to be kept private.

"I'm committed to the Cowboys until the end of 2029 and I think it's a bit silly that you have to get up here and speak to a bit of nonsense that's going around."

Dearden made it clear that he was "not recommitting".

"I've always been committed to the Cowboys and none of that has ever changed, so it's a bit disappointing that my partner and family have had to deal with a lot of questions," he said.

Maroons dealt massive blow Queensland selectors have been forced to cope with the news one of their best playmakers will miss up to eight weeks with his ankle injury.

"It's had an impact on the personal life. I've got a pregnant partner and I think when there's speculation getting around like that, people are reading that and it gives them questions to ask and you always have to answer to people."

Dearden has played just once since suffering a syndesmosis and ankle fracture in round 10.

The injury ruled him out of the State of Origin series and he returned against the Dolphins in round 20 only to tear a muscle in his shin on the other leg.

Dearden played through the match but during the following week discovered the issue.

"It's been a frustrating year having to sit out because I love representing the Cowboys," Dearden said.

"It's a bit of a weird injury but it's tracking pretty well and hopefully I've only got a few more weeks [on the sidelines]."

Dearden and the club have targeted the round 26 home clash with Wests Tigers in Townsville as his return date, after the Cowboys' round 25 bye.

North Queensland is in ninth position and plays Gold Coast away on Thursday night before an away clash with Parramatta without its influential half.

AAP

World.title: Police hunt for offenders after alleged assault on Camp Sovereignty
World.content:
Activists from Melbourne's Camp Sovereignty say they have been deeply traumatised after a member of their group was assaulted at the Indigenous protest site.

On Sunday night, Ash Ni Mara, 37, was allegedly attacked by two strangers attempting to extinguish the campfire.

“I’m feeling pretty shattered and scattered and quite bruised,” said the Gunai, Gunditjmara and Palawa person.

" I'm feeling shocked because it came out of nowhere, I was feeling angry too. "

The attack occurred at the First Nations protest site, Camp Sovereignty, in Melbourne. It’s the second time within 12 months that people at Camp Sovereignty have allegedly been attacked.

Camp Sovereignty member Ash Ni Mara was allegedly assaulted at the central Melbourne site over the weekend. (ABC News)

Ash told the ABC that the female perpetrator entered the site filming on her phone, while the male started to pull pieces of the wood out of the sacred fire and throw them around.

"I was sitting with one of our sisters who was pregnant ... and one of our aunties who is elderly and has some mobility issues, so I got up to respond,” Ash said.

“I went up to him and said, ‘what are you doing’ and he said it was an illegal fire.”

Ash said they were then dragged six metres before being held in a headlock and repeatedly hit.

"Others that were here went to restrain him so that he would stop trying to assault me," Ash said.

Ash was treated on site by paramedics who checked them for concussion and minor facial injuries.

The two perpetrators fled on foot before the police arrived.

Ash is known as a fire protector, a volunteer who maintains the continuous fire at Camp Sovereignty.

The camp is located in Melbourne’s CBD, in the Kings Domain parklands.

It started in 2006 as a protest against the Commonwealth Games. In 2024 the sacred flame that sits at the centre of the site was reignited, using ashes transported from the Aboriginal Tent Embassy in Canberra.

It’s a sacred and significant site for First Nations people, and is where the remains of 38 Indigenous people were buried after being repatriated from the Museum of Victoria.

The site is maintained by volunteers as a part-protest and part-vigil, caring for the country where ancestors are buried.

Founder says attack “very disturbing”

Camp Sovereignty founder Krautungalung elder Robbie Thorpe said he was constantly worrying about the site.

“To be woken up in the middle of the night and be told that people have been assaulted is a real concern,” he said.

Camp Sovereignty co-founder Robbie Thorpe (ABC News)

Mr Thorpe said the fire is an “important part of Aboriginal culture”.

“It’s symbolic of our law and of our culture … it’s kept alive permanently, [and] this is the way we connect with our ancestors and culture,” he said.

" This is a place of peace … it's very important to us all. "

Mr Thorpe explained when the fire is desecrated “it’s really disturbing”.

"We don’t really know where this violence is coming from so that’s a worry, otherwise we get on famously with everyone that comes here.”

Mr Thorpe said they are going to think of what security the camp has in place going forward.

Police still searching for alleged perpetrators

Superintendent Zorka Dunstan told the ABC that police are considering the attack to be racially motivated.

“At this stage we potentially are, but will confirm that once we understand the motive,” Superintendent Dunstan said.

Camp Sovereignty began in 2006 as a protest against the Melbourne Commonwealth Games. (ABC News)

Police patrols were unable to locate the offenders, and are currently canvassing CCTV within the area.

“We aren’t sure who they are at this point in time, but we have our Melbourne CIU investigating,” she said.

Superintendent Dunstan said police are likely to lay assault charges.

“Once we determine what’s applicable or what's appropriate we will make those known,” she said.

Second attack within 12 months at the site

On Wednesday, in Victoria’s County Court, four men charged over last year’s attack on Camp Sovereignty pleaded guilty.

Jaeden Johnson, Zack Dewaard, Blake Cathcart and Timothy Lutze pleaded guilty to one charge each of violent disorder, with Johnson and Lutze also pleading guilty to committing an indictable offence while on bail.

Last week, in Victoria’s County Court, four men charged over last year’s attack on Camp Sovereignty pleaded guilty. ( ABC News: Danielle Bonica )

The men have all been associated with the National Socialist Network (NSN), a now disbanded, far right group.

The court heard that on August 31, after attending a “March for Australia” protest, the men were part of a wider group who stormed the camp, carrying sticks and flagpoles, and advancing despite being told to leave.

The men are accused of shouting racist and sexist slurs, and attacking individual camp members in groups of two or three.

A number of people were injured in the incident, one suffering a fractured nose while others had cuts and bruising.

The men’s lawyers argued they should receive a non-custodial sentence.

World.title: Former Sea Eagle, ABC radio personality John Gibbs diagnosed with cancer
World.content:
Former Manly-Warringah Sea Eagles halfback and ABC Sport rugby league commentator John Gibbs has been diagnosed with cancer.

Gibbs, 70, has been part of the ABC Sport team since 2016 and has been a popular personality among listeners.

ABC NRL Daily podcast Andrew Moore and the ABC NRL team bring you your daily dose of NRL conversation. The team give you the context and depth beyond the headlines.

He was on the ABC Sport call with Andrew Moore and Matthew Elliott on Sunday afternoon when the Parramatta Eels defeated Wests Tigers.

"Gibbsy", who played 81 first grade games for the Sea Eagles and represented New South Wales and Australia, announced his diagnosis on Monday, and that he would be stepping away from broadcasting to focus on his health.

Moore, ABC Sport's lead rugby league caller, said his friend Gibbs wanted listeners to know he was prepared for his upcoming treatment on NRL MONDAY.

"John Gibbs called me this afternoon to confirm something he had been fearing for a while. He's been diagnosed with cancer — Hodgkin's lymphoma," Moore said.

"He knows he's in for a fight, but he wants you to know he's up for it.

"We are family and, as I discovered a year ago, the wave of support from the ABC team, it's significant, it's powerful, it's amazing and it helps.

"Like so many of you, he's ready to kick cancer to the kerb and beat the mongrel."

The former international has been a constant on Sydney radio since the 1980s as a commentator, presenter, and host for 2UE, 2GB and ABC Sport.

World.title: Young Tiger banned as gut-punch crackdown continues
World.content:
Richmond defender Luke Trainor has received a one-match ban for striking as the AFL's crackdown on gut punches continues.

Trainor will miss the Tigers' trip to face Adelaide at Adelaide Oval on Saturday after punching West Coast forward Jack Williams in the stomach as the two were jostling in the goal square at the MCG on Sunday.

Williams dropped to the turf while Trainor jogged off.

Coach Adem Yze had hoped Trainor would only be fined for the second-quarter incident in the 11-point win over the Eagles.

But the match review officer took a dim view of the incident, assessing it as intentional conduct, medium impact and body contact, which draws a one-match ban.

It leaves Richmond short of a tall defender against Adelaide's powerful forward line headlined by Riley Thilthorpe.

AAP

World.title: Former prison worker found guilty of raping inmate
World.content:
A former prison worker has been found guilty of the rape and aggravated indecent assault of a female inmate at an Adelaide jail.

Enio Screpanti, 67, stood trial in South Australia's District Court for four days after pleading not guilty to the offences, which occurred in the early 2020s.

After just over two hours of deliberations, the 12-person jury delivered unanimous guilty verdicts to the charges.

Screpanti's family became audibly and visibly emotional as the jury's verdicts were read aloud.

After the verdicts, prosecutor Christine Hanna asked the court to revoke Screpanti's bail due to the seriousness of the offending.

Screpanti's defence barrister Gilbert Aitken opposed the application, but Judge Anne Barnett said it was appropriate Screpanti be remanded in custody and revoked his bail.

A District Court jury unanimously found Enio Screpanti guilty of rape and aggravated indecent assault. (ABC News: Che Chorley)

In closing submissions earlier on Monday, Ms Hanna had told the jury the victim was a "credible and reliable witness".

The jury previously heard Screpanti sexually assaulted the woman on a treadmill in the prison gym before raping her several months later after asking "[her] to come to a shed as they had a job to do".

Convicted murderer, and fellow inmate, Nicole McGuinness also gave evidence in the trial about uncharged acts that were brought before the court to give context to the charged offending.

"On the prosecution case that evidence still has a part to play in your [the jury] consideration and deliberations on the charged acts," Ms Hanna said in her closing address.

"It might also help you to understand that the alleged charged acts did not come out of the blue."

World.title: End of the super-cycle: Big call on the national property market
World.content:
PoliticsFederalProperty prices End of the super-cycle: Big call on the national property market Shane Wright August 3, 2026 — 11:59pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A 30-year property super-cycle that has made Australian homes among the most expensive in the world may finally be coming to an end, one of the nation’s top economists has predicted, despite warnings prices will eventually rebound due to a chronic shortage of homes. AMP chief economist Shane Oliver on Monday said a combination of higher interest rates, record-poor affordability, a slowdown in immigration and the federal government’s budget changes to property taxation may have finally ended a cycle that has pushed home prices way above fair value. A 30-year surge in house prices may be coming to an end, according to Shane Oliver. Dion Georgopoulos Data released by Cotality this week showed the national property market at its weakest point since the Albanese government came to office in 2022, with capital city values falling by 0.9 per cent last month. House values in Sydney dropped by 1.7 per cent while they edged down another 1.4 per cent in Melbourne. But every major capital city market is now either slowing or has turned negative.



Despite the downturn, national values have retreated only to their March levels, while the median house values in Sydney, Brisbane, Perth, Adelaide and Canberra all remain above $1 million. Related Article Analysis

Property prices Sliding housing prices gave the Reserve Bank a surprise helping hand Oliver said a range of factors, including the decline in official interest rates since the early 1990s, had contributed to a property super-cycle that had pushed up property prices across the country well above their long-term value. But with interest rates staying higher, the government removing key property tax concessions, the commitment by both sides of politics to ease immigration and a property market that was unaffordable for many potential buyers, that super-cycle had probably ended. Oliver believes instead of sharp increases over the coming decade, property prices are likely to tread water.



“If the property super-cycle upswing is over, it could mean a decade or so of real house prices ranging sideways and a moderation in home price-to-income ratios,” he said. “It could also mean that cyclical downturns in property prices are deeper and upswings take longer for prices to reach new record highs.” AMP chief economist Shane Oliver. Oscar Colman Oliver expects a 7 per cent easing in prices through to next year. Even after that, property values in every capital city will still be well above their long-term fair value. He estimates Sydney property values are 41 per cent above their long-run price levels, with Brisbane values are 65 per cent higher. Even in Melbourne, the nation’s weakest property market, values are 25 per cent above their long-term trend.



But Oliver said prices could step up given the ongoing shortage of housing across the country. That’s a view shared by KPMG chief economist Brendan Rynne, who will on Tuesday forecast a nationwide drop of 1.1 per cent in house prices this year before rebounding by 3.4 per cent in 2027. KPMG is expecting house values in Sydney to fall 4.4 per cent this year before lifting 3.6 per cent next year, while in Melbourne, it believes a 5 per cent drop in 2026 will be partially recovered by a 3.3 per cent lift in 2027. Even after this year’s price correction, KPMG’s Brendan Rynne is expecting house prices to climb again through 2027. Eamon Gallagher Both Brisbane and Perth are expected to experience house price increases of 3.6 per cent next year after lifting by 4.6 per cent and 6.4 per cent respectively this year.



Rynne said higher interest rates, affordability pressures and a decline in investor activity were behind the drop in prices this year. But a dearth of homes meant the property market would go through a “V-shaped” recovery. “While demand has weakened, Australia’s underlying housing issues are stronger than ever,” he said. “Australia continues to face a housing shortage. Population growth remains firm, rental vacancy rates are still exceptionally low and housing supply is still well below demand.” Deputy Liberal leader Jane Hume said the entire property market was being upended by a shortage of houses, higher rents and now “uncertainty” for first time buyers and investors.



Related Article Housing slump ‘Price reduced’: The polarising strategy some vendors use in a downturn She suggested the drop in prices was a deliberate action of the government through its budget measures. “I wonder whether this was an intentional or an unintentional consequence of Labor’s housing taxes,” she told News24. Treasurer Jim Chalmers said the decline in values so far this year was similar to seven previous falls in the property market that have occurred over the past 20 years, including episodes in 2022 and between 2017 and 2019. He said people bought homes as a long-term investment rather than focused on a short-term easing in prices.



“People don’t make investments in housing from day to day or week to week, month to month, and so from time to time you will see movements in prices like these,” he told ABC radio. “But housing is a long-term investment, and we continue to expect over the course of the coming years that prices will continue to rise, but more modestly than before.” Cut through the noise of federal politics with news, views and expert analysis. World.title: An accolade from beyond the five-mile limit
World.content:
For the sake of the sound of sensation across the nation, Geoff Gilligan of Coogee would like to thank Herald culture scribe Karl Quinn: “Your article on Bill Oddie (July 30 ) answered a question that comes into my head about every decade. It regarded a skit on a TV show that featured a pirate radio station that had only one record. I hadn’t been able to remember the program. Karl’s tribute mentioned that it was from an episode of The Goodies. The tune was A Walk in the Black Forest (aka Eine Schwarzwaldfaht), by Horst Jankowski.” Granny always wished they’d made good on Graeme’s scheme for a Pirate Church of England.

“I share Helen Lewin’s frustration with the dubbing of English films (C8),” says Elizabeth Savage of Hughes (ACT). “In Italy in the ’60s, my friend and I were delighted to find the latest Doris Day/Rock Hudson movie playing locally. Imagine our disappointment when we discovered they could both speak fluent Italian.”

Paul Taylor of Winston Hills would like to nominate “the Water-Rats or, if you prefer, the Rakalis as the name for the Australian Underwater Hockey Team (C8). The rakali is the size of a small possum, with a distinctly white-tipped tail that is slightly shorter than the body. They are well adapted to their aquatic lifestyle and use their large, partially webbed hind feet as paddles while their thick tail operates like a rudder. Myth has it that they have a distinctive cry when travelling through murky water – ‘We’re the Rakali!’”

“One of the Australian teams should, of course, be called The Down-Unders,” adds Helen Howes of Collaroy.

Sticking with sport, the wise Chris Commens of Rosebery reckons “we can be grateful that Victoria piked out of funding the Commonwealth Games. The medal tally is so bountiful that if held here, this would have been seen simply as massive home-team advantage. Branch stacking of a different order. Credibility is thankfully restored by competing overseas.”

World.title: Police, protesters descend on One Nation fundraiser in Hawthorn East
World.content:
A substantial police presence greeted protesters seeking to express their dissatisfaction with Pauline Hanson at a One Nation party fundraiser, just hours after the party unveiled its upper house candidates for the upcoming Victorian election. Hanson delivered a speech at Hawthorn East’s Tower Hotel on Monday night. A reporter from this masthead was unable to gain entry to the fundraiser. One Nation’s party leader Pauline Hanson arriving at Tower Hotel in Hawthorn East. Joe Armao Police in riot gear were on hand as a large crowd, chanting and holding signs, demonstrated outside the venue. The hundreds of demonstrators chanted “Nazi scum off our streets” towards the One Nation contingent inside, as well as anger towards Hanson’s billionaire friend Gina Rinehart. One banner held by protesters said, “Unite to fight the right” and “Campaign against racism and fascism”.



The protesters became particularly animated when it appeared Hanson left via the adjoining bottle shop’s drive-through just before 8pm. Protesters at the event. Joe Armao One Nation’s Victorian party leader Warren Pickering arrives at Tower Hotel Joe Armao Dozens of police stared at them in silence from over road barriers, after closing parts of Burwood and Camberwell roads to manage the contingent. “Victoria Police respects the right to protest lawfully, however we ask people to do so peacefully without impacting the broader community,” officers said in a statement.



Crowds queue to see Hanson at the Tower. Joe Armao Protesters were heavily outnumbered by the police presence, which reportedly included federal police, in Hawthorn East. Joe Armao Before the event, Hanson addressed the protest action on Channel Nine. “I’m not interested in what they have to say, have your say at the ballot box, I really don’t care,” she said, adding she planned to return to Victoria “a few other times” before election day. View post on X



“You might have Ben Carroll as your premier,” Hanson told the meeting: “But he doesn’t instil confidence in me when he speaks…” “He’s not my Premier!” roared an attendee in reply. Hanson with supporters. Joe Armao The One Nation leader addresses the crowd. Joe Armao Hanson mingles with attendees. Joe Armao



Speaking on 3AW, pub owner Joe Ramoro said he did not hesitate to host One Nation despite this recent history. “I’m not worried at all to be honest. Some of my customers can’t get in to play the pokies. Senator Hanson attracts these protests seemingly everywhere she goes,” he said. One Nation laader Pauline Hanson, state president Warren Pickering and other party candidates on Monday. Jason South Earlier in the day, Warren Pickering was announced as the One Nation leader in the lower house, defending the party’s decision to keep under wraps for another month its policies and full list of candidates it will take into the November election. The decision means voters will have just three months before the election to scrutinise an organisation which has never been a serious player in Victorian politics but on Monday declared its ambition to govern the state.



Pickering, who unsuccessfully ran for the Senate in the 2025 federal election and as a candidate in the 2022 state election and who joined Pauline Hanson’s anti-immigration movement after retiring from the Australian Defence Force, said the decision not to divulge policies and candidates was taken to maximise the party’s “strategic advantage”. He on Monday indicated that part of this strategy was to preserve campaign funds until closer to the November 28 poll. “We have got to play our cards close to our chest,” he said. “The major parties are out there spending valuable energy, effort and resources to go backwards in the polls. Hanson refused the ABC, The Age and The Guardian entry to Monday’s event. Jason South “We’ll continue to roll out our candidates as we see fit.”



Pickering, who also serves as One Nation’s state president in Victoria, will contest the semi-urban lower house seat of Pakenham, which was held by Labor at the 2022 election by just a few hundred votes. “We are officially putting the major parties on notice,” Pickering said. “We intend for this to be a November to remember and we are contesting to govern.” A large police presence was outside the press conference in case protesters gathered. Jason South The unorthodox approach to campaigning – which normally involves parties maximising the opportunity for voters to get to know a party’s policies and candidates – extended to Hanson’s decision to block several major media outlets from attending Monday’s press conference called to announce Pickering’s leadership. The ABC, The Age and The Guardian were all refused entry to the event staged at Melbourne’s Savoy Hotel.



Pickering issued a pre-emptive threat to sue media companies which published or broadcast “blatant character assassination attempts” of candidates. Photo: Matt Golding Hanson said it was the first time she had denied the ABC entry to one of her press conferences. “I am not putting up with the spin gotcha moments, wanting to have a go at me, or treat us totally different to what you do the other major political parties,” she said. “Enough is enough. So they’re banned.” Two ABC regional reporters were ejected from a One Nation press conference on May 8 during campaigning for byelection for the federal seat of Farrer.



Pickering is One Nation’s second confirmed lower house candidate behind Darren Hercus, the small business owner who stood for the party in this year’s Nepean byelection. One Nation on Monday announced seven upper house candidates who, polls suggest, are all likely to be elected. Hanson, Pickering and Darren Hercus, One Nation’s candidate for the seat of Nepean, in April, during campaigning for the Nepean byelection. Simon Schluter The line-up includes: Colleen Harkin, a former member of the Liberal Party’s administrative committee who took her own party to court for loaning former state leader John Pesutto $1.55 million to pay his legal costs to Moira Deeming and avoid bankruptcy.

Mark Nicholson, the creator of One Nation’s anti-woke film Super Progressive Movie and a co-founder of the animation house Stepmates Studios, which creates Hanson’s cartoon web series Please Explain.

One Nation’s only Victorian state parliamentarian, Rikki-Lee Tyrrell, who will recontest her Northern Victoria seat. Mark Nicholson, the creator of Pauline Hanson’s A Super Progressive Movie, is a One Nation candidate for the Victorian upper house.



Geelong councillor and former police officer Chris Burson, who at the last election stood for the Angry Victorians Party which sought to undermine anti-lockdown sentiment for electoral gain.

Political newbies Fiona Lopez, Aaron Sandford and Natalie Adams. Hanson said her party intended to stand candidates in every state seat. “People want change in their state, and they’re crying out for that change,” she said. “They don’t trust the major political parties at all. They don’t believe what they’re delivering is the answer to it.” Hanson was dismissive of last week’s decision by Victorian Labor to move against former premier Jacinta Allan and install Ben Carroll as the new state leader. “They have just moved the decks on the Titanic,” she said, interrupting her new state leader to make the remark. Loading



Pickering described the coming political contest in apocalyptic terms. “We are on the precipice of social and economic collapse and anyone who doesn’t believe that is simply not paying attention,” he said. Pickering said his party’s “core” policies on farming, energy and cost of living would be announced at the end of August, along with the names of the party’s other 86 lower house candidates. Pauline Hanson on Monday. Jason South So far, the party has promised, if elected, to abolish Victoria’s treaty with its First Nations People, establish a royal commission into Big Build corruption and hire more police and open more police stations. They are all policy positions shared with the Coalition.



One Nation has announced a significant change to its backroom operations nationally, with Hanson’s long-time chief of staff, James Ashby, promoted to national director. Ashby spent more than a decade as Hanson’s closest adviser and helped to professionalise the party. Chris Taylor, who recently worked as chief of policy at the Australian Banking Association, will become Hanson’s chief of staff. With Lachlan Abbott, Fiona Byrne Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Defence rejects cover-up claims on Taipan chopper crash
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts Defence rejects cover-up claims on Taipan chopper crash Tess Ikonomou August 3, 2026 — 8:28pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Senior military officers have denied the Defence department covered-up parts of an investigation into a fatal Taipan helicopter crash that killed four soldiers. Captain Danniel Lyon, Lieutenant Maxwell Nugent, Warrant Officer Class Two Joseph Laycock and Corporal Alexander Naggs were killed when their MRH-90 chopper crashed off Queensland’s Whitsunday Islands during Exercise Talisman Sabre on July 28, 2023. The ADF members who died in the 2023 tragedy, remembered during an earlier hearing. AAP Air Vice-Marshal Tim Innes, representing the Defence Aviation Authority, told a parliamentary inquiry on Monday there was a full aviation investigation safety report publicly available. “I’m not aware of any cover-up of any sort,” he told the public hearing in Canberra.



Former Taipan test pilot, retired Major Ian Wilson, previously told the inquiry the Defence Flight Safety Bureau’s investigation couldn’t be trusted and had been “corrupted”. The Defence Flight Safety Bureau’s investigation found the primary cause of the accident was “spatial disorientation”, which occurs when a pilot misperceives the position of their aircraft in relation to the surrounding environment. In an opening statement, Air Vice-Marshal Innes acknowledged last Tuesday marked the third anniversary of the crash. “Their loss continues to be felt deeply by the families, friends, teammates, units, and the broader army and defence community,” he said. “We pay our respects and acknowledge the enduring impact of this tragedy on their families and all those affected.”



Greens Senator David Shoebridge grilled the officials about the “significant fatigue” the pilots were experiencing and how army aviation managed the safety issue. In response, Commander Army Aviation Command Major-General David Hafner said the ADF was constantly looking at the schedule of activities to make sure personnel were able to take time off. “Really looking through a lens of cumulative fatigue, and making sure that personnel are afforded activities through the annual schedule of events to take leave as part of fatigue management as well,” he said. Australia’s work health and safety regulator has referred two briefs of evidence to the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions relating to fatigue management and the TopOwl helmet system worn by the pilots. Comcare officials told a previous inquiry hearing Defence should face prosecution.



Sue Lyon, the stepmother of Captain Lyon, said she had no confidence in the investigative processes of Defence and “there appears to have been a determination from the outset to attribute responsibility for this accident to Danniel through a finding of human error”. “From the time of Danniel’s crash, the Department of Defence has shown little empathy or consideration towards the families of the pilots involved,” her written statement to the inquiry reads. “As a grieving stepmother, I have personally witnessed and experienced behaviour from Defence personnel that I consider unacceptable, insensitive and dismissive.” The inquiry’s report is due in early September. AAP

World.title: Police, protesters descend on One Nation fundraiser in Hawthorn East
World.content:
A substantial police presence greeted protesters seeking to express their dissatisfaction with Pauline Hanson at a One Nation party fundraiser, just hours after the party unveiled its upper house candidates for the upcoming Victorian election. Hanson delivered a speech at Hawthorn East’s Tower Hotel on Monday night. A reporter from this masthead was unable to gain entry to the fundraiser. One Nation’s party leader Pauline Hanson arriving at Tower Hotel in Hawthorn East. Joe Armao Police in riot gear were on hand as a large crowd, chanting and holding signs, demonstrated outside the venue. The hundreds of demonstrators chanted “Nazi scum off our streets” towards the One Nation contingent inside, as well as anger towards Hanson’s billionaire friend Gina Rinehart. One banner held by protesters said, “Unite to fight the right” and “Campaign against racism and fascism”.



The protesters became particularly animated when it appeared Hanson left via the adjoining bottle shop’s drive-through just before 8pm. Protesters at the event. Joe Armao One Nation’s Victorian party leader Warren Pickering arrives at Tower Hotel Joe Armao Dozens of police stared at them in silence from over road barriers, after closing parts of Burwood and Camberwell roads to manage the contingent. “Victoria Police respects the right to protest lawfully, however we ask people to do so peacefully without impacting the broader community,” officers said in a statement.



Crowds queue to see Hanson at the Tower. Joe Armao Protesters were heavily outnumbered by the police presence, which reportedly included federal police, in Hawthorn East. Joe Armao Before the event, Hanson addressed the protest action on Channel Nine. “I’m not interested in what they have to say, have your say at the ballot box, I really don’t care,” she said, adding she planned to return to Victoria “a few other times” before election day. View post on X



“You might have Ben Carroll as your premier,” Hanson told the meeting: “But he doesn’t instil confidence in me when he speaks…” “He’s not my Premier!” roared an attendee in reply. Hanson with supporters. Joe Armao The One Nation leader addresses the crowd. Joe Armao Hanson mingles with attendees. Joe Armao



Speaking on 3AW, pub owner Joe Ramoro said he did not hesitate to host One Nation despite this recent history. “I’m not worried at all to be honest. Some of my customers can’t get in to play the pokies. Senator Hanson attracts these protests seemingly everywhere she goes,” he said. One Nation laader Pauline Hanson, state president Warren Pickering and other party candidates on Monday. Jason South Earlier in the day, Warren Pickering was announced as the One Nation leader in the lower house, defending the party’s decision to keep under wraps for another month its policies and full list of candidates it will take into the November election. The decision means voters will have just three months before the election to scrutinise an organisation which has never been a serious player in Victorian politics but on Monday declared its ambition to govern the state.



Pickering, who unsuccessfully ran for the Senate in the 2025 federal election and as a candidate in the 2022 state election and who joined Pauline Hanson’s anti-immigration movement after retiring from the Australian Defence Force, said the decision not to divulge policies and candidates was taken to maximise the party’s “strategic advantage”. He on Monday indicated that part of this strategy was to preserve campaign funds until closer to the November 28 poll. “We have got to play our cards close to our chest,” he said. “The major parties are out there spending valuable energy, effort and resources to go backwards in the polls. Hanson refused the ABC, The Age and The Guardian entry to Monday’s event. Jason South “We’ll continue to roll out our candidates as we see fit.”



Pickering, who also serves as One Nation’s state president in Victoria, will contest the semi-urban lower house seat of Pakenham, which was held by Labor at the 2022 election by just a few hundred votes. “We are officially putting the major parties on notice,” Pickering said. “We intend for this to be a November to remember and we are contesting to govern.” A large police presence was outside the press conference in case protesters gathered. Jason South The unorthodox approach to campaigning – which normally involves parties maximising the opportunity for voters to get to know a party’s policies and candidates – extended to Hanson’s decision to block several major media outlets from attending Monday’s press conference called to announce Pickering’s leadership. The ABC, The Age and The Guardian were all refused entry to the event staged at Melbourne’s Savoy Hotel.



Pickering issued a pre-emptive threat to sue media companies which published or broadcast “blatant character assassination attempts” of candidates. Photo: Matt Golding Hanson said it was the first time she had denied the ABC entry to one of her press conferences. “I am not putting up with the spin gotcha moments, wanting to have a go at me, or treat us totally different to what you do the other major political parties,” she said. “Enough is enough. So they’re banned.” Two ABC regional reporters were ejected from a One Nation press conference on May 8 during campaigning for byelection for the federal seat of Farrer.



Pickering is One Nation’s second confirmed lower house candidate behind Darren Hercus, the small business owner who stood for the party in this year’s Nepean byelection. One Nation on Monday announced seven upper house candidates who, polls suggest, are all likely to be elected. Hanson, Pickering and Darren Hercus, One Nation’s candidate for the seat of Nepean, in April, during campaigning for the Nepean byelection. Simon Schluter The line-up includes: Colleen Harkin, a former member of the Liberal Party’s administrative committee who took her own party to court for loaning former state leader John Pesutto $1.55 million to pay his legal costs to Moira Deeming and avoid bankruptcy.

Mark Nicholson, the creator of One Nation’s anti-woke film Super Progressive Movie and a co-founder of the animation house Stepmates Studios, which creates Hanson’s cartoon web series Please Explain.

One Nation’s only Victorian state parliamentarian, Rikki-Lee Tyrrell, who will recontest her Northern Victoria seat. Mark Nicholson, the creator of Pauline Hanson’s A Super Progressive Movie, is a One Nation candidate for the Victorian upper house.



Geelong councillor and former police officer Chris Burson, who at the last election stood for the Angry Victorians Party which sought to undermine anti-lockdown sentiment for electoral gain.

Political newbies Fiona Lopez, Aaron Sandford and Natalie Adams. Hanson said her party intended to stand candidates in every state seat. “People want change in their state, and they’re crying out for that change,” she said. “They don’t trust the major political parties at all. They don’t believe what they’re delivering is the answer to it.” Hanson was dismissive of last week’s decision by Victorian Labor to move against former premier Jacinta Allan and install Ben Carroll as the new state leader. “They have just moved the decks on the Titanic,” she said, interrupting her new state leader to make the remark. Loading



Pickering described the coming political contest in apocalyptic terms. “We are on the precipice of social and economic collapse and anyone who doesn’t believe that is simply not paying attention,” he said. Pickering said his party’s “core” policies on farming, energy and cost of living would be announced at the end of August, along with the names of the party’s other 86 lower house candidates. Pauline Hanson on Monday. Jason South So far, the party has promised, if elected, to abolish Victoria’s treaty with its First Nations People, establish a royal commission into Big Build corruption and hire more police and open more police stations. They are all policy positions shared with the Coalition.



One Nation has announced a significant change to its backroom operations nationally, with Hanson’s long-time chief of staff, James Ashby, promoted to national director. Ashby spent more than a decade as Hanson’s closest adviser and helped to professionalise the party. Chris Taylor, who recently worked as chief of policy at the Australian Banking Association, will become Hanson’s chief of staff. With Lachlan Abbott, Fiona Byrne Be the first to know when major news happens.

World.title: Defence rejects cover-up claims on Taipan chopper crash
World.content:
NationalQueenslandCourts Defence rejects cover-up claims on Taipan chopper crash Tess Ikonomou August 3, 2026 — 8:28pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Senior military officers have denied the Defence department covered-up parts of an investigation into a fatal Taipan helicopter crash that killed four soldiers. Captain Danniel Lyon, Lieutenant Maxwell Nugent, Warrant Officer Class Two Joseph Laycock and Corporal Alexander Naggs were killed when their MRH-90 chopper crashed off Queensland’s Whitsunday Islands during Exercise Talisman Sabre on July 28, 2023. The ADF members who died in the 2023 tragedy, remembered during an earlier hearing. AAP Air Vice-Marshal Tim Innes, representing the Defence Aviation Authority, told a parliamentary inquiry on Monday there was a full aviation investigation safety report publicly available. “I’m not aware of any cover-up of any sort,” he told the public hearing in Canberra.



Former Taipan test pilot, retired Major Ian Wilson, previously told the inquiry the Defence Flight Safety Bureau’s investigation couldn’t be trusted and had been “corrupted”. The Defence Flight Safety Bureau’s investigation found the primary cause of the accident was “spatial disorientation”, which occurs when a pilot misperceives the position of their aircraft in relation to the surrounding environment. In an opening statement, Air Vice-Marshal Innes acknowledged last Tuesday marked the third anniversary of the crash. “Their loss continues to be felt deeply by the families, friends, teammates, units, and the broader army and defence community,” he said. “We pay our respects and acknowledge the enduring impact of this tragedy on their families and all those affected.”



Greens Senator David Shoebridge grilled the officials about the “significant fatigue” the pilots were experiencing and how army aviation managed the safety issue. In response, Commander Army Aviation Command Major-General David Hafner said the ADF was constantly looking at the schedule of activities to make sure personnel were able to take time off. “Really looking through a lens of cumulative fatigue, and making sure that personnel are afforded activities through the annual schedule of events to take leave as part of fatigue management as well,” he said. Australia’s work health and safety regulator has referred two briefs of evidence to the Commonwealth Director of Public Prosecutions relating to fatigue management and the TopOwl helmet system worn by the pilots. Comcare officials told a previous inquiry hearing Defence should face prosecution.



Sue Lyon, the stepmother of Captain Lyon, said she had no confidence in the investigative processes of Defence and “there appears to have been a determination from the outset to attribute responsibility for this accident to Danniel through a finding of human error”. “From the time of Danniel’s crash, the Department of Defence has shown little empathy or consideration towards the families of the pilots involved,” her written statement to the inquiry reads. “As a grieving stepmother, I have personally witnessed and experienced behaviour from Defence personnel that I consider unacceptable, insensitive and dismissive.” The inquiry’s report is due in early September. AAP

World.title: Who's feeling job market recovery? And where has downturn hit hardest?
World.content:
It has been a tough few years to be a jobseeker. Data this week is expected to show the unemployment rate still hovering around the highest level it's been in a decade.

But fortunes have varied depending on where you are in the country, and the type of work you do.

The job market peak was reached in October 2023, when there were 2.395 million filled jobs nationwide. The trough was in October last year, when that had dropped to 2.337m.

Provisional estimates are that the number is now about 2.35m filled jobs.

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub said from the peak of the market to the bottom, there were just under 60,000 jobs lost but since then, 17,575 have been recovered, leaving the country still 40,924 jobs short compared to the busiest time in the labour market.

Here are some of the winners and losers of the labour market both since the peak, and over the past five years.

Sectors

Since the job market peaked in October 2023, the biggest drop in jobs in percentage terms has been felt in the information media and telecommunications sector, down 11.2 percent or 3761 jobs.

Over five years, smoothing out the post-Covid high, job numbers in that sector are still down 5.6 percent.

Construction has also had a sharp fall from the peak, having lost 8.4 percent of its jobs, or 17,249, but the number is flat compared to 2021.

What's good debt, what's bad debt and how do I tell the difference? No Stupid Questions with Susan Edmunds Download MP3 11m

Some sectors have continued to grow since the peak, such as arts and recreation services, which is up 6.1 percent from 2023 and 16.2 percent over five years. Of this sector, the largest proportion of jobs is in sports and physical recreation, such as people working in gyms. Their numbers have lifted from 22,700 in 2023 to 24,400 last year. There has also been significant growth in businesses. Personal health and fitness training business numbers increased 112.5 percent between 2019 and 2025.

Healthcare and social assistance jobs have also increased since the job market peak, up 5.4 percent since 2023 and 12.7 percent from five years ago.

Education and training is up 4.4 percent from the peak and 6.6 percent over five years.

Eaqub said, on a per population basis, there had not yet been any real recovery. Data would show there were more hours being worked, he said, but the recovery in jobs so far had only kept pace with population growth. "It's not a high-quality recovery yet."

Simplicity chief economist Shamubeel Eaqub. RNZ

Construction's increase was the largest in number terms, followed by manufacturing down 11,822.

Westpac chief economist Kelly Eckhold said the strongest parts of the labour market were those that were tied to underlying population growth.

"It's the expansion of certain elements of public service-related industries as well, particularly in health, education… those sectors have grown a lot because the population has grown in the last five years. They've continued to grow, albeit at a slower rate since 2023, because that was when the population growth peaked… there's quite a few industries that are a lot more government or public sector dominated, and they just tend to not be really influenced by the cycle so much."

In contrast, sectors such as construction were much more closely tied to the fortunes of the wider economy.
